brief.open:
The Off Switch — the short read

Condenses §0 · §19

Welcome. This is the Brief — the short read, the door into the record, written for the reader who has not opened the ledger and does not plan to. Nothing here assumes prior context; it asks minutes and repays them with the essentials.

One observation shapes everything else. Every institution that outlived its own usefulness shared a single trait: by the time everyone could agree it should stop, no path remained to stop it. The off switch is therefore not an appendix to this project — it is the opening subject. A system built to serve people over long horizons must first demonstrate that those same people can end it.

The Brief answers four questions, in order. What was built — the platform and the legal shields around it. How the money unwinds — what happens to the reserve if the system ever stops. Why the platform exists at all — the purpose all the machinery serves. And what is still wrong — the open faults, stated plainly rather than filed away.

One structural promise before you continue. Every sentence on this page is replayed from the same append-only ledger that produces the full record. The Brief and the ledger are not two documents that someone must keep in agreement; they are two orderings of one body of entries, so they cannot drift apart.

A boundary, stated once. What follows is analysis and architecture only — never advice on legal, tax or investment matters. No security is offered here, no token, no investment — nothing solicited, nothing marketed, anywhere in this document. Every financial figure here is illustrative — demonstrating a formula, never projecting a result.
brief.flaw:
What was built, and the flaw that prompted it

Condenses §C · §4 · §7 · §16

Vision 2525 is built to last five hundred years. Say it aloud and a specific danger arrives with it — and for a long stretch, we built our way straight into that danger without noticing.

The framework carries five legal shields, each answering a way institutions are killed from outside. No equity: no shares, so the system cannot be bought. An asset lock: value that enters can never be extracted. Federated domestic personality: the framework lives as separate legal persons in separate countries, so no single government can shut it down — and under the survivor standard, the United States entity, seated in Texas, is the designated last body standing should the others fall. Recognition that cannot be purchased: standing inside the system is earned, never sold. And a funded reserve behind every promise, so commitments are cash-backed rather than hopeful.

Together, these five make the system extraordinarily hard to stop from outside. Read the list again and notice what is absent.

That absence is the flaw. Five defences against outsiders ending this system — and none for the people inside it who might need to end it. That is no durable institution. It is the silhouette of every organisation that ceased to be useful yet could not be stopped. And we assembled it while congratulating ourselves on the shields.

The framework as it stands closes that gap. Anyone may petition to turn the system off. The vote runs unweighted — one person, one vote — and nothing anyone contributed counts toward it, including money. If the vote carries, the reserve unwinds along a published formula; obligations already earned are honoured in full; whatever remains is locked inside a trust only a genuine restart can open. The shields protect the system from others; this provision protects the people inside it from the system.
brief.gates:
Three gates

Condenses §7

Ending the system is not one decision. It is three decisions, in strict order, by three kinds of authority — and knowing who holds each gate tells a newcomer where power sits.

Gate one is the mandate, and it belongs to every enrolled person, voting unweighted. The bar is deliberately high: a 40% quorum, a 60% carry, and the same result confirmed 180 days later — because one angry season should not end a five-hundred-year undertaking, though a settled conviction should.

Gate two is the counter-signature, held by the tri-council with the Innovation Leader among its members: two-thirds must sign, and the Leader’s assent has to sit inside that two-thirds.

Gate three is execution: the master admin account, under two keys, carries the decision out. Note the verb — carries out, never makes. Gate three is ceremony, not choice. The decision was already complete at gates one and two.

Why tolerate a personal veto at all? Because it is a brake, never a throttle. The Innovation Leader can slow or halt a shutdown; nothing at gate two can start one. No pairing of leader and council, however unanimous, can end this system unless ordinary people have first carried the mandate. The veto is structurally incapable of destroying the framework — its only power is to preserve it against a decision it judges premature. That asymmetry alone makes a single-person veto acceptable in a document this suspicious of concentrated power.

And even so, it expires — twice over. The counter-signature is tied to the founding 7 + 3 term, lapsing on its own ten years from the moment cumulative Seed Token proceeds first reach $1,000,000. The veto lapses sooner if it sits unexercised for ninety days after a carried mandate, because an off switch that can be defeated by declining to pick up the phone was never an off switch at all.
brief.formula:
The formula, in plain terms

Condenses §6 · §7 · §15

Innovation growth has one measure — the Qualified Innovation Score, QIS = (R + GP + OI + ERD) ÷ 4; its growth ΔQIS sizes the reward pool and mints no 웃. Distinct from the shutdown Index below.

Suppose the vote carries and the system stops. What happens to the money?

What does not happen: the reserve is not a pot divided among whoever argues loudest. It splits into three pools, in strict order, and the first claim does not belong to a funder.

First comes the guarantee pool — illustratively $173,982,600. This is contribution already earned by participants, paid in full, always. It is never distributable. Second comes the holder pool — illustratively $239,948,806 — which repays Seed Tokens (bought once at $1.036, the entry membership floor, distinct from 웃 earned live) — split by the Continuity Index described below. Third comes the Continuity Trust — illustratively $86,068,593 — which gathers unclaimed shares and residue and opens only on a valid restart. The figures assume an illustrative reserve of $500,000,000; free reserve equals reserve minus committed obligations, $326,017,400, and its unclaimed portion falls to the Trust.

Why does the guarantee outrank every funder? Because it must outlive the vote. Contributors elect a payout horizon of one, three or five years. A contributor two years into an elected five-year payout schedule does not forfeit the remaining three because a majority swung. A guarantee that a majority can cancel is not a guarantee — and a shutdown is exactly when breaking that promise would be cheapest. So it is ranked first, ahead of everyone.

The holder pool divides by the Continuity Index, and its logic is plain: Seed Token holders are repaid in step with how much the platform grew across the years their money was funding it. Growth is read through four measures, weighted equally — Revenue, Gross Margin (gross profit as a share of revenue), Operating Income and R&D Spend. For each measure m, Δm(y) is the value in the year the system stops minus the value in the year you bought. Divide by the same difference measured from the founding year: your share of the climb. Your Index is the average of the four shares. Your payout is your tokens multiplied by your Index, taken as a share of everyone else’s.

An early holder funded the entire climb, so their index sits near 1.0. Someone who arrived in the final year funded only the last stretch, so theirs is low. And someone who bought the day the system stopped funded none of the climb, so their index is exactly zero.

Why differences, not a growth multiple? Dividing revenue today by revenue in your buy-year breaks at once: operating income runs negative in the early years, and dividing by a negative number (−144.0) flips a founder’s claim into a debt. Differences pass cleanly through zero, orderly from the first holder to the last.

Worked: Adaeze, year 1, 100 tokens, index 0.9958, $333,649 per token. Sokha, year 4, 10 tokens, 0.9108, $305,178. Mireille, year 8, 1,000 tokens, 0.5902, $197,746. Tomas, year 11, 100 tokens, 0.1742, $58,375. Mireille takes the largest total; Adaeze, ten years earlier, earns nearly six times as much per token.
brief.restart:
If it comes back

Condenses §7 · §13

The strangest clause in this framework: what happens if it ever comes back. A restart, here, is deliberately not a reversal. If switching the system back on could simply undo the vote that ended it, that vote would be theatre — a pause anyone with patience and capital could outlast. The design places real, structured distance between an ending and any return.

The distance begins with dormancy. Following a shutdown the system sleeps for one, two or three years, and which of the three is decided by a random draw from the final state hash — the cryptographic fingerprint of the last state recorded. That randomness carries the whole argument. A restart date announced in advance becomes a date to organise around: capital parked against it, coalitions assembled to meet it, the return timed to suit a political season instead of genuine readiness. Since no one can predict the draw, no one can position for it. Add one preparation year onto the drawn period and you have the earliest possible return.

Then the condition that matters most. The system that was switched off is precisely the system no one may bring back. Whoever petitions for a restart must arrive holding a concrete improvement, and the returning version must differ from the ended one in at least one ratified way. Note what this is not: not a promise, not a request for anyone’s trust. It is a mechanical comparison between two releases, in the open, and if it comes up empty — nothing demonstrably changed — the restart is void, however sincere its petitioners.

Together, these rules turn an ending into something rare among human institutions. To end this system is not to kill it, and it was never meant to be. It is a forced cycle of learning, carrying a real cost: time, reflection, and one proven improvement before anything returns.
brief.risk:
The risk this platform addresses

Condenses §1 · §2 · §3 · §5 · §6

Everything above is machinery, and a newcomer may fairly ask what it serves. This section is the answer.

Generating ideas is something large groups do superbly; choosing among them is something they do poorly. No shortage of intelligence explains this. What explains it is that the choosing process gets captured by whoever holds the most of some scarce thing — money, tenure, volume, or nearness to the decision. What comes out wears the look of consensus and is nothing of the kind. Ideas from contributors who lack standing never surface, and once anyone measures the outcome, the decision has become unattributable: no one to credit, no one to hold to account.

Each failure meets a specific counter-rule here, worth a slow walk-through.

Capture. Whoever funds a thing normally steers it. Here, money receives and never decides; no contribution purchases a vote — not at any price, not in any amount.

Invisible dissent. Objections ordinarily appear only after the fact, disguised as failure. Here every person contributes in their own language, so an objection enters the record before the vote rather than after it.

Unattributable outcomes. Normally no one can say whose idea succeeded. Here each contribution is a ledger entry carrying an author, a time and a reason.

Uncompensated contribution. Value tends to flow toward whoever owned the platform. Here contributed time earns a unit settling at local rates, beneath a hard annual ceiling no one may exceed.

Geographic discounting. An hour of a life is ordinarily worth less according to where it was lived. Here an hour mints identically everywhere; settlement alone is local. And where the framework pays survivors, every life is priced at one generous benchmark — the USA/Texas standard — never a local one.

Institutional immortality. Most institutions cannot be stopped after they stop working. Here an off switch exists, and everything above describes it.

Compressed to a sentence: this platform lets a group decide together without the outcome being quietly purchased, see who gave what, and dissolve the arrangement once it stops serving them. Keep that list in mind; the rest of the brief is implementation.

The economic half deserves precision — it is where such frameworks most often quietly fail. Contributed time mints its unit of recognition at one rate for the whole earth — a single full-time year of work lands exactly on the annual ceiling, whether that year happened in Lagos or Seattle. The local wage enters only at settlement, the moment a unit becomes money, and that wage is frozen at the instant the work was recorded, beyond re-pricing by any later holder.

The ordering matters, and we know because we got it wrong. Our own code long brought the local wage in at the wrong point. Result: the identical ceiling demanded 29,409 hours in Nigeria against 614 in Washington State — a 47.9× spread, from a framework whose declared purpose is helping as many people as possible reach that ceiling. The figure now stands at 2,080 hours everywhere. We discovered the flaw, published it, and repaired it, and this brief tells you so deliberately: a framework reporting nothing but its successes is not really reporting.
brief.open_items:
What we are still getting wrong

Condenses §8 · §19

No honest introduction closes on its achievements, so this one closes on what remains unsolved. Five items stand open. Three await a human decision; two are operational and closable within the week. All five sit in the ledger’s own defect register — entered by us, in the open, not left for someone else to find. If that seems an odd welcome, consider it the most honest one a framework can offer.

First, a late funder can be wiped out by the payout. The index drops to zero in the shutdown year, building a perverse incentive: the moment shutdown begins to look probable, the rational funder stops funding — the reserve drains, and shutdown grows more probable still. Self-fulfilling, and timed for the worst conceivable moment. The remedy — a principal floor applied ahead of the index split — has been proposed and awaits adoption.

Second, the shutdown thresholds remain unratified. Quorum, carry and confirmation exist as proposals only, and a threshold without ratification is no threshold. Council ratification is all this needs.

Third, the reserve sits below its long-horizon target. A corpus holding nine years of security for a billion people lies beyond any founding treasury alone; only long-run compounding closes that distance. Under current law each survivor elects a payout of one, three, or five years, priced at the USA/Texas survivor standard — exactly why the sizing question cannot be waved aside. What it needs is a funding decision: pre-fund in full, or match funding to duration.

Fourth, two caps carry no numbers. Overhead and institutional gifts are each described as capped, yet no figure is stated. A cap without a number is no cap. The fix is publishing the numbers.

Fifth, credential hygiene on the master key. It is held to best-in-class standards: an alphanumeric passcode, multi-factor authentication, a hardware-bound physical key, lockout on failed attempts, and rotation before first use. What is published is the standard, not the secret; the standard is the accountable part.

The disclosure rule of this framework holds that a gap kept hidden does more harm than a gap made known — and that it binds its own authors first. Read this list as evidence the rule is real.

What we ask for, then: three decisions, ordered by how much each blocks. One — the principal floor: should a late funder have their contribution returned before the growth-indexed split takes effect? Our answer is yes, but since this alters a stated rule, the alteration is not ours to make. Two — the five shutdown thresholds: until fixed, the off switch stays a specification, not a working mechanism. Three — the reserve fork: pre-fund the guarantee whole, or let funding track the duration of obligations as each arises.
brief.why:
Why any of this is possible

Condenses §5 · §9 · §11

By now a reasonable reader is entitled to skepticism. An off switch, a random dormancy, a mandatory improvement before restart — these are expensive promises. What makes them affordable? A system can only carry an off switch if being stopped does not destroy it, and this one survives stopping for a structural reason worth understanding first: the record is never stored, only reconstructed.

Every release of this framework can be rebuilt exactly, inside any ordinary browser, from an append-only record of changes — including the version running the day the system was switched off. Nothing is ever overwritten. No correction erases the mistake it corrects; the error and its repair sit side by side in the same list, permanently. The history keeps its scars in plain view. And because every version is a replay of the same list, any two versions can be compared directly, difference by difference.

That property makes ending the system survivable rather than final. A framework intended to run five centuries will be wrong along the way — realistically, more than once. The design question was never how to prevent being wrong; no honest engineer would claim that. The question was whether error could be made recoverable, and reconstruction is the answer: the past cannot be lost, so it can always be returned to, examined, and built upon.

Here the brief offers something better than an argument — a demonstration, because this document is proof of its own claim. Every word you are reading replays out of the same append-only ledger that carries the complete record. Drag the slider and the brief itself moves through its releases like everything else; press ⇆ Compare and you can audit what changed in it between any two points.

There is also a confession folded into that demonstration. The brief once lived as a separate file beside the main document, and within a day of the main document being renamed, the two had drifted far enough to need hand-patching. That is precisely the failure this framework exists to prevent — divergent copies of one truth — reproduced inside our own deliverables. The remedy was structural, not cosmetic: one document now stands with two doors, never two documents telling the same story.

So the answer to the skeptic runs in one line. The off switch is affordable because nothing here can be destroyed by using it; the record beneath every promise is rebuilt from an unerasable history, and you are holding a working sample of that history — welcome, and read on.
mot.thesis:
“We Can Not Master What We Are Not Aware Of”

2022

The sentence is deliberately not about intelligence, and it is not a complaint about anyone. It is a statement about records. A thing that is never written down cannot be governed, cannot be corrected, and cannot be argued with. It can only be repeated.

Most institutional failure works this way. Someone saw it. It was not recorded in a form that survived the person who saw it. The decision came round again, was taken again by people who could not see that it had already failed, and the second failure was blamed on judgement rather than on the absence of a record.

Everything mechanical in this document exists to make that sentence operable rather than admirable: what is recorded, who may read it, and whether the record survives the people it embarrasses. The third condition is the one that decides the other two.
front.thesis:
What this is

A tool for self-governance. Not a party, not a company, not a country — an attempt to actually execute an idea most of the world already claims to hold.

We the People. Not we the corporations, and not we the wealthy.

The phrase is three hundred years old and almost every constitution has a version of it. The difficulty was never the sentence. It was that a people has no instrument with which to govern itself at scale — no way to record what its members contribute, weigh what they think, and fund what they choose, without handing the pen to whoever already owns the press.

This document describes that instrument, and the working parts exist. An hour of a human life as the unit (§1). A ceiling nobody may pass, including the authors (§2). Money may fund and may never govern, by any route (§3). A record that outlives the people who built it (§5). An off switch that belongs to the people rather than to us (§7).

Four beats, and what each one is for

Three readers outside this work reviewed it separately and each stopped at the same line. It said three things where the framework does four, and the fourth was the one carrying the most weight.

BeatWhat it doesWhere it lives
The UnitContribution is measured — an hour of a human life, priced by the region’s own published minimum wage, so an hour in Phnom Penh and an hour in Austin are compared honestly rather than converted.§1
The ShieldRights are protected by structure rather than by promise. Nobody may accumulate past the ceiling, money may fund and may never govern, and these hold against the authors first.§2 · §3
The LedgerHistory is preserved. The record is append-only: a mistake is corrected by writing the correction, never by editing the mistake, so the reasoning survives alongside the outcome.§5 · §8
The ReplayVerification happens without permission. Any person may reconstruct the entire record from any point in its history and check it themselves, with no account, no key and nobody to ask.§13
Four purposes, not three. Compressing them loses the one that does the most work.
● Why the fourth beat is not a feature

Replay is easy to mistake for a playback control, and one reviewer said so directly. It is not. Replay is the answer to the oldest problem in governance, which is that a record kept by an institution can only be checked by asking that institution. Every audit, every disclosure regime and every freedom-of-information law is a workaround for the same asymmetry: the keeper decides what the checker sees.

Truth that can be replayed does not require belief. The file you are reading rebuilds every earlier version of itself in front of you, offline, with no server involved. That is not a demonstration of the idea. It is the idea, running. A framework that asks to be trusted has already lost the argument; one that can be re-derived by a stranger five centuries from now never has to make it.

🔒 Two conditions on everything that follows
Entirely voluntary
Nobody is enrolled, assigned, defaulted in or signed up by someone else. A person gives an hour because they chose to, and stops when they choose to. A framework for self-governance that begins with compulsion has already answered the question it claims to be asking.
Trust is earned in public, in real time
Not asked for, not asserted, and not borrowed from a credential. Every release is published as it happens, every earlier release stays readable, every defect is listed by number including the ones found after shipping, and the shortfall is stated in the same place as the progress. Anyone may check the arithmetic without permission from us.

Those two conditions are why this is slower than a manifesto and why it might survive one. A thing people join freely and can audit continuously does not need anybody to believe in it first.

Why the unit comes first

Every governance framework that pays people eventually collides with the same fact: an hour of a person’s life is worth wildly different amounts of money depending on where they were born, and any system that ignores that is either unaffordable in rich countries or insulting in poor ones.

Most schemes resolve this by picking one currency and one rate, then quietly excluding everyone the rate does not suit. This document takes the opposite route. It defines a unit of recognition that is denominated locally and compared globally, so that the same contribution earns the same recognition everywhere while settling into money that actually buys groceries where the contributor lives.

Get the unit wrong and nothing downstream can be fixed: the ranking is skewed, the budget is fiction, and the people doing the work in the lowest-wage regions are silently written out. Get it right and the rest of the architecture has something honest to stand on.

This document has become three things, in the order a reader needs them. A unit anyone on earth can be paid in, with a ceiling that protects everyone from what accumulation does to governance. A structure nobody can buy, seize, or switch off, built from things permanently given up rather than arguments to be won. And a way of arriving in a jurisdiction that does not require anyone to be frightened first.

The parts are in that order because that is the order in which they fail. A framework with no unit cannot pay anyone. A framework with a unit and no shield gets taken. A framework with both and no way of arriving gets stopped by someone who first heard of it in a complaint.
front.mission:
Mission, vision, outcome

Confidence is not a tone. It is what a reader feels when they can check the claim themselves. So this section states what we are trying to do, where it goes, and — the part usually left out — how anyone would know if it failed.

Mission · what we do, every day

Shorten the distance between a human intention and funded, measured work — for anyone, anywhere, in their own language, with the record surviving everyone involved.

Vision · where this goes

A world in which the ability to contribute is not gated by where a person was born; in which what someone contributes is recognised in a unit that means the same thing on every continent and settles into money that buys food where they live; in which no accumulation of wealth, no corporation and no government holds more governing authority than one human being; and in which the record of all of it is still readable in the year 2525 by someone with no connection to anyone who built it.

Objective outcome — eight numbers

Every one is published, every one has a threshold that would constitute failure, and every one has a component that computes it. An objective with no failure condition is a wish.

OutcomeMeasured asSuccessFailureOwner
ReachShare of full-time-equivalent contributors reaching 9,999 웃≥ 0.80< 0.60Cube 9
Guarantee fundedRing-fenced reserve ÷ committed instalments≥ 1.00< 1.00, unpublishedCube 8
Worth fundingReturn on contribution, retrospective, per region≥ 1.00< 1.00Cube 9

ReadableLanguages live with a complete key set33 / 33< 33 after N=99Cube 2

Human-signedIrreversible acts carrying a human signature100%any exceptionCube 25
Six of the eight are computable from mechanisms already specified in this document. Two — reserve coverage and settlement latency — are specified precisely enough to build and are not yet built. That distinction is stated rather than blurred.

Notice what is not on the list. Money raised is not an outcome; it is an input. Number of participants is not an outcome; it is a means. Neither appears, because a framework that measures itself by what it collects will eventually optimise for collecting.

Checkpoints

YearCheckpointWhat must be true
2027Ground zeroAustin: one person contributes, is recognised, and is settled, end to end. All eight metrics published, however small the numbers.
2030CityOne million participants. Reserve coverage at or above 1.00. Thirty-three languages live.
2050FederationDomestic legal personality in twenty-plus regions. No single government able to switch it off.
2125Beyond the foundersTen leadership handovers completed. Nobody involved at the beginning is still alive. It still works.
2525The horizonThe record from 2026 still replays, still reconciles, and is still readable by someone with no connection to anyone who built it.
The 2125 checkpoint is the real test. Anything can be sustained by the people who cared enough to start it. Only a structure survives their absence.
Why you can have confidence in this

Not because it is well argued. Arguments are cheap and this document has been wrong twice already.

Because every mechanism is marked implemented, specification-only or proposed, and you can check which. Because the defects are published, including the one where our own code contradicts our own rule. Because every correction stays visible in the ledger — scrub back and find the errors exactly as we shipped them. Because the replay runs in your browser rather than asking for your trust. And because there is a failure threshold beside every success number above, which is the one thing nobody writes down unless they intend to be held to it.

§0 · THE HOW ↑ contents

§0   Vision • 2525 is the WHAT. This is the HOW.

Which of the thirteen layers this document actually answers. The eight it does not

Vision • 2525 is a civilization coordination framework set out in thirteen diagrams. It states what a coordinated civilization needs: humanity at the centre, a recursive operational core, resilient communications, coordination that survives scale, intelligence at the edge, preserved operational truth, one spatial reality, rehearsal before deployment, collective intelligence guiding distributed action, balanced governance, qualification before scale, an adoption cycle, and continual evolution.

That is the what. It is deliberately architectural, and it does not specify how a single hour of a single person’s contribution becomes a payment, a record. A vote that money cannot buy.

This document is the how — for five of those thirteen layers.Three more it touches partially. Four it does not answer at all, and one it deliberately contradicts. All of that is in the table below rather than left for a reader to discover.

The map

Five answered, three partial, four not addressed, one divergent. Publishing the four we do not touch is what makes the five worth reading.

The one place we disagree

⇆ Diagram 12 — a genuine fork, not an oversight

Vision 2525’s adoption flywheel runs on aligned capital: investors deploy capital with confidence, fund innovation, drive impact. It is a careful, well-governed model and it is a reasonable answer.

This document has no investors at all. No equity exists, nothing appreciates, nothing trades, and there is no instrument to buy. Funding is 1/7 of an hour at a time from people who receive a permanent public record and nothing else. That is slower by orders of magnitude and it forecloses the entire adoption engine diagram 12 describes.

Both answers are defensible: one trusts governance to hold for five centuries, the other refuses to depend on it holding. We assumed honesty cannot coexist with something valuable to own, and paid in speed. Anyone who thinks we are wrong should build the other one — the fork stays written down for comparison.

What this means for a reader of the thirteen diagrams

If you came for…Start at
Diagram 01 — how a person is actually counted§1 The Unit and §2 The Ceiling and the Floor
Diagram 06 — replay and operational truthThe Ledger view. It is the mechanism, running.
Diagram 10 — governance that holds under pressure§3 The Wall and §4 The Shield
Diagram 11 — qualification before scale§10 The Present, where we score ourselves and fail
Diagram 12 — adoption and capital§4 The Shield, the renunciation, where investor funding was refused and what it cost
Diagrams 03, 05, 07 — comms, edge, spatialNot here. Those layers are open, and this document neither claims nor blocks them.
The two documents are complementary, not competing — provided each says which question it answers. This section exists so neither has to be read as claiming the other’s ground.
front.constitution:
THE CONSTITUTION ↑ contents

The Constitution

Ten principles. Everything in the nineteen sections that follow is downstream of these, and each one names the section where it is actually implemented — a constitution that cannot be checked against a mechanism is a preamble.

Why any of this exists. Organisations keep their conclusions and lose the thinking that produced them, so a failure understood once is met again years later by people with no way of seeing that it already happened. Every principle below, and every mechanism the nineteen sections describe, is an answer to that one problem. Set out in full at §8.

 PrincipleWhere it lives
IHumanity remains sovereign.
Any natural person may petition to end this framework, and the vote is one person one vote, unweighted. Nothing anybody contributed counts. The people who funded the reserve vote with exactly the same single vote as someone who has never given a cent.		§7
IIAuthority shall always be reviewable.
Authority is bounded by term rather than by promise: one ten-year standing, seven years leading and three mentoring with none, with recall available throughout. The mentoring years make succession a scheduled event rather than a crisis.		§9
IIIThe record cannot be secretly altered.
The ledger is append-only and there is no delete operation. A mistake is corrected by writing the correction, never by editing the mistake, so the reasoning survives beside the outcome and an error stays checkable at the release where it was made.		§5
IVNo intelligence supersedes human dignity.
Artificial and shared intelligence advise; human intelligence decides. No model, no metric and no majority may reduce a person to an input, and the ceiling binds the authors before it binds anyone else.		§18
VNo institution owns civilization.
The founders renounce, in writing and in advance, every mechanism by which they could come to own this: no supervoting class, no founder allocation, no reserved seat, no perpetual role.		§4
VIParticipation must remain voluntary.
Nobody is enrolled, assigned, defaulted in or signed up by someone else. A person gives an hour because they chose to and stops when they choose to. A framework for self-governance that begins with compulsion has already answered the question it claims to be asking.		§19
VIIEvidence outranks opinion.
Every claim about the running system cites a file and a line and is marked built, specified or proposed. Identical inputs must produce identical outputs, and the proof runs in the reader’s own browser rather than on our word.		§13
VIIIQualification precedes scale.
Nothing moves to the next phase because it is popular. It moves because it passed a gate that was published before the attempt, and the framework is deliberately slower than it could be for exactly this reason.		§17
IXEvery generation inherits the ledger, and nothing else.
The record passes on in full — every decision, every reason, every correction. Accrued value does not: no position, no claim and no accumulated advantage survives the person who earned it. What is inherited is the ability to check the past, never a head start over the present.		§5 · §1
XNo single actor may capture the framework.
Money may fund and may never govern, by any route, at any price. Contribution buys no vote, no weight and no say, so capture by capital is structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged.		§3
Nothing here is new. Every principle was already load-bearing somewhere in the record; what was missing was the root they all descend from. If a principle and its section ever disagree, the section governs — the mechanism is the commitment, and this page is the summary of it.
🔒 What a constitution is for here

Not to inspire. To make capture expensive. Each principle names a specific thing that cannot be done, by us first: we cannot outvote you on ending this, cannot hold authority past ten years, cannot edit an error out of the record, cannot buy a vote with money, and cannot leave our children a position instead of a ledger.

A framework whose founders have not written down what they are forbidden to do has not been designed — it has been announced. These are the ten things we gave up in order to ask anyone for an hour.
paper.s1:
§1 · THE UNIT ↑ contents

§1   The Unit

The centre

Begin with what you were given. Not what you earned, not what you inherited, not what any border permits — what you were given. Before money, before nations, before anyone thought to price a life, there was the hour: the one endowment issued to every human being at the same rate. The pharaoh and the ferryman held it equally. A parent rocking a child in the small hours spends it now, and the engineer drawing a city for the year 2525 will hold no more. There is a guide within you — older than any economy — that has always known this, which is why unfairness about time stings in a place unfairness about things cannot reach.

Then we built instruments that price everything, and let them price the one thing that was never theirs. Watch a single Tuesday. In Lagos, a nurse completes a procedure; in Austin, a second nurse completes the same procedure with the same skill; and the world files those two hours apart by the twenty-one-fold gap we politely call economics. Nothing in the hour changed. Nothing in the skill changed. Only the ground beneath each nurse changed. Ask what an hour of work is worth and every answer describes a country, never the hour. Say the true name: a measurement error — one we agreed, generation after generation, not to correct. And an error, unlike a sin, asks for no punishment. It is the one form of injustice that surrenders to arithmetic.

So the correction begins smaller than expected: it measures again. One hour of attention, given, is written down as one unit of recognition — a receipt for a portion of a life, never an asset, never for sale, never inherited, because a record of what you did stops being yours the moment another hand can hold it. The ceiling stands at nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine per person per year — one full working year at the minimum wage of your own region, deliberately a livelihood and never a fortune. The reference multiple beneath it, four point eight zero seven, was chosen by nobody — nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine over two thousand and eighty working hours, division, not committee. When a number here looks designed, rerun the arithmetic yourself. A definition a child can re-derive from a calculator and a published wage is the kind a civilisation can carry five hundred years — and the kind no power on Earth can confiscate.

Hold the whole arc in one breath. Past: your ancestors counted by their place before their person. Present: two nurses on one Tuesday, and a ledger that finally counts the person before it consults the place. Future: children of 2525 rebuilding this unit and finding it unchanged, the way corrected errors always look obvious afterwards.

What this page hands you is not a feeling. It is a standing possibility: the next hour you give — to a patient, a child, a stranger, a field — can be recorded as exactly what it was, one hour of a human life, equal to every other hour, anywhere, without anyone’s permission. Your share of the one universal endowment was issued at your birth and renews at dawn. Whether it enters the record is now yours to decide, and no one else’s.

Needs

Ask a hundred people what an hour of their work is worth and you will get a hundred numbers, none of which describe the hour. They describe the country. A nurse in Lagos and a nurse in Austin can perform the identical procedure with identical skill on the same Tuesday, and the world will price those two hours over twenty-one times apart. We have grown so used to this that we call it economics rather than what it is, which is a measurement error we have agreed not to correct. Every attempt to build something fair on top of money inherits that error at the foundation, and no amount of good governance above it can undo an arithmetic mistake underneath.

Outcomes

When contribution is counted in hours, two people who did the same work hold the same record. Not the same purchasing power, which no framework can promise and none should, but the same recognition of what they did. That single change makes it possible to compare effort across a border without first agreeing on a currency, which is why every other mechanism in this document can exist at all. The person is counted before the place is consulted.

Solution

One hour of human attention becomes one recognition unit. The ceiling is nine thousand nine hundred and ninety nine of them per person per year, which is what one full working year produces at the minimum wage of the region a person lives in — 웃 is a multiple of that wage, and the entry price is that same wage divided by seven — and it is deliberately livelihood rather than fortune. Nothing purchases units. Nothing inherits them. They confer no vote, no weight, no priority, and they cannot be traded, because the moment a record of what someone did becomes a thing someone else can hold, it stops being a record of what someone did. The unit is a receipt, not an asset, and the difference is the whole design.

Evidence

The reference multiple is four point eight zero seven, arrived at by division rather than by choice: nine thousand nine hundred and ninety nine divided by two thousand and eighty working hours. One full-time year therefore lands exactly on the ceiling, which is not a coincidence but the definition. The ceiling is what a year of a life is worth here, and everything above it rolls forward rather than accumulating. When a number in this document looks designed, check whether it is simply what the arithmetic produced. Usually it is, and where it is not, we say so.
front.locked:
The locked definition

웃 Authoritative · Document 0 · class: Immutable
  • 웃 is denominated in multiples of local or regional minimum wage.
  • Higher multiples are allowed.
  • Hard annual ceiling: 9,999 웃 per natural person.
  • Goal: enable as many people as possible to reach 9,999.
  • Earned value is paid as the contributor elects — in real time, streamed at a dollars-per-minute rate as it is earned, up to the 9,999 웃/yr maximum rate; or over a term of one, three, or five years — guaranteed for the elected term; five where none is elected.
  • Measurement of Time holds every payout to that annual maximum rate, so no one exceeds it; anything earned above it rolls forward to the next period — the next week, the next year.
  • Purpose: livelihood security and continuity — not lump-sum wealth.
⚠ What “guaranteed” is backed by

The bullets above are the operator’s words and are not edited. This note is the reading, because a reader who stops at the fifth bullet reads a promise, and the fifth bullet is where they stop.

Earned value is paid out over the elected term — one, three, or five years — funded by a ring-fenced reserve whose balance is published monthly. The guarantee is structural, not aspirational. A coverage ratio below 1.00 is published the month it occurs, in every signatory language. If the reserve cannot carry new earning, new earning slows and committed instalments are untouched — which is the difference between this and every historical promise that was not kept. The reserve rule is specified and unbuilt, and §15 publishes what it will cost.

This is the authoritative definition for Document 0 and for all future governance language. Every clause in this document is downstream of it. Where an earlier write-up conflicts, this text governs.

Two readings that have appeared in expert commentary are both wrong and are corrected here. 웃 is not a literal count of hours — 9,999 hours is more than a person is awake for in a working year. And it is not a free-floating abstraction — without the minimum-wage anchor it loses the property that makes it equitable. It is a multiple of a local hour, and the multiple is where skill, scarcity and responsibility are expressed.
unit.denom:
Denomination: the local hour is the anchor

The base unit is fixed by definition:

1 웃 (base)  =  one hour at 1x the contributor’s local minimum wage
M            =  the multiple applied to that contributor’s hour
웃 earned     =  M x hours

The anchor is local; the unit is universal. A contributor in Lagos and a contributor in Austin doing the same work at the same multiple earn the same number of 웃. What differs is what a 웃 settles into — and that is correct, because a naira and a dollar buy different things in the places they are spent.

This is the split that makes the whole system work: recognition is global, settlement is local. Confusing the two is the defect described later in this document.
unit.multiples:
Multiples: how the ceiling becomes reachable

The locked definition says higher multiples are allowed and that the goal is to enable as many people as possible to reach 9,999. Those two clauses together settle a question the earlier write-ups left open, and the answer falls straight out of arithmetic.

Multiple MHours to reach 9,999In full-time yearsWhat this band is for
1x9,9994.81Unreachable in a year. The floor of the scale, not a working band.
2x5,0002.40Entry contribution; part-time and learning participation.
3x3,3331.60Sustained competent contribution.
4.807x2,0801.00The reference multiple. One full-time year lands exactly on the ceiling.
6x1,6660.80Scarce skill, or responsibility carried.
8x1,2500.60Rare expertise; the band where part-year work still reaches the ceiling.
10x+≤1,000≤0.48Exceptional contribution. Permitted, published, and still capped at 9,999.
The ceiling divided by a standard working year gives 4.807. That number is not chosen; it is what 9,999 and 2,080 imply. It is the multiple at which a full year of full-time contribution reaches the ceiling exactly.
The design consequence

Higher multiples do not let anyone earn more — the ceiling is identical for everyone. They let people reach the ceiling sooner, and on fewer hours. A surgeon at 10x and an apprentice at 2x can both arrive at 9,999; the surgeon needs a thousand hours and the apprentice needs five thousand. The multiple recognises scarcity. The ceiling refuses to convert scarcity into power.
unit.ceiling:
The ceiling, and why it is hard

9,999 웃 per natural person per year — the Texas vintage settles at $72,492.75, though that dollar value tracks each contributor’s local minimum wage and is not universal. Not per role, account, or organisation — per person. The figure is the governing default under current policy, amendable through governance, not a fixed constant.

The denomination, and what 9,999 counts

1 웃 (base) = one hour at 1× the contributor’s local minimum wage. A multiple M applies for qualified contribution, so 웃 earned = M × hours — 100 qualified hours at M = 2.5 earn 250 웃, while actual time worked stays 100 hours. The local hour is the anchor; 웃 has one denomination, not two. M is unbounded, but the annual 웃 PAYMENT is bound at 9,999 with excess rolling forward — higher leverage reaches a stable year sooner, focusing on stability first.

Actual time is recorded separately, minute by minute, by Measurement of Time (MoT). So 9,999 웃 per year is the annual settlement boundary under operating policy (recognition itself is unbounded) — not 9,999 hours worked, nor a limit on contribution history. MoT and Replay preserve every recorded minute and contribution; nothing earned or evidenced is erased. Record, policy, and legal settlement are three separate things, and applicable law controls when pay is due.

A hard ceiling is unusual and deliberate: concentrated wealth is the mechanism of governance capture, not a side effect — a system able to pay one person a fortune manufactures, from its own treasury, the very actor it was designed to resist. The ceiling removes that possibility by construction, not policing.

The ceiling does not limit contribution. A person may contribute far past 9,999 웃 of recognised value in a year; the record stays permanent and complete. What stops at the ceiling is settlement, not recognition.

How 웃 is earned and drawn — the intended live mechanics

These describe the target settlement rail — the design, not yet the shipped backend

The mechanics below are the specification, not a claim every step already runs. Classification, withholding and payment frequency resolve per local law at settlement; 웃 accrual does not itself assert an employment or contractor relationship.

웃 is earned live, per minute, in local money

웃 is designed to accrue continuously at 웃/min while a person works a project, each minute translated to the contributor’s own local currency at that minute’s rate. Recognition is never a lump sum on a date; it is a balance growing minute by minute, shown in plain local currency and decimal alongside the ledger notation below.

The project pre-funds the work

A project pre-pays the task’s whole block of work — a task known to be, say, 100 웃 for a region is paid in full up front by the commissioning party — into a ring-fenced, real-time payments escrow before work begins, so every 웃/min accrued is funded as it accrues, not promised against fundraising. Each draw releases only the earned-to-date balance; the unearned remainder returns on early exit.

The contributor sets the payment terms

The contributor ELECTS the payout mode — real-time (accrue at 웃/min, draw from escrow as achieved) or deferred over one, three or five years. Under real-time, how and when to draw belongs to the contributor:

  • Manually — draw the current earned balance whenever wanted.
  • Automatically at a threshold — set a 웃 level; the balance releases each time it is reached.
  • On demand, several times a day — up to a governing default of five draws a day (policy, not a constitutional constant), for same-day cash.

The unit notation — N.mmmm..ssss, Base-3600

The internal ledger grammar — shown beside a plain-currency figure

Every coin — 웃 (H.I.), ♡ (S.I.), ◬ (A.I.) — and the time and currency behind them are settled and stored in one positional notation, mirroring the Celestial-2525 A.B..C coordinate: N.mmmm..ssss — a whole number, dot, Base-3600 sub-unit, double dot, Base-3600 sub-sub-unit, each fractional group running 0000 to 3599, 3600 reserved as rollover to the next whole. The contributor always sees a plain local-currency figure beside this ledger form.

  • N — whole units: full tokens, hours, or currency.
  • mmmm — major sub-unit, 0000 to 3599. For 웃, whose whole unit is an hour, this is the second: an hour holds exactly 3,600, so Base-3600 nests the hour directly into seconds, no separate sixty-minute level.
  • ssss — minor sub-unit, 0000 to 3599: one part in 3,600 of the major sub-unit (for 웃, a fraction of a second).

100.3599..3599 is one hundred whole units carrying 3,599 major and 3,599 minor sub-units; 10000.3599..3599 is ten thousand whole tokens, same tail. A full unit completes at rollover: 100.3600..0000 is the non-canonical form of 101.0000..0000, as Celestial-2525 reads a full orbit as 3600. Base-3600 is native to time — an hour holds exactly 3,600 seconds, so 웃’s major sub-unit is second-exact by construction; the same grammar placing a planet on its orbit places a contributor’s moment on the clock and their ◬, ♡ and 웃 in the ledger.

Overflow past the 9,999 웃 annual default rolls forward, never lost. But where earned 웃 is wages under local law, wage-payment timing follows that law and overrides any deferral — the ceiling caps the scheme’s annual settlement default, never a worker’s legal right to be paid for work already done.

Decision D10 — the ceiling never suspends wage law

The 9,999 웃/yr boundary is a settlement ceiling on recognition, not a rate floor, and never suspends mandatory wage law; each jurisdiction’s 웃 base rate is the greater of the eXeL 1/7-hour reference and the current statutory minimum. Per The two tranches, wage-regulated engagements split into a wage-floor tranche — paid on the mandated cadence, exempt from the cap and rollforward — and an acceleration tranche, alone subject to the ceiling. Only statutory-wage classifications route through the floor; voluntary Shared Intent participation stays outside wage law by the canon’s own definition, and no legally owed minimum wage is ever deferred by rollforward.

Decision D5 — anti-sybil without surveillance

Ordinary participation — Seed membership, ♡ contribution, 웃 accrual through POD-witnessed work — requires no identity disclosure; sybil-resistance comes from the Seed’s non-transferable recurring cost and the POD’s witnessing requirement, audited for collusive vouching, never personal data. Only at annual settlement, as 웃 nears the 9,999 boundary and converts to cash, does the system require a privacy-preserving proof of unique personhood: a one-time, zero-knowledge attestation from an accredited third party that this is one human claiming one ledger, storing only a pass/fail token, never a biometric record. This reuses the identity scrutiny cash settlement already carries under law, capping the ceiling per person, not pseudonym.

HI max, and the accrual ledger

9,999 웃/year is the maximum; across 525,600 minutes that is 0.0190239726 웃/min, shown in the A.B..C grammar as 0.0068..1751 (Base-3600) and viewable over a 91-day or 365-day window in 웃/min → $/min → local currency/min. Every accrual carries a Measurement-of-Time triple — (unit, Start, Duration): the $ amount, the Start (day/time/minute), and the Duration in N.mmmm..ssss. The same amount settles real-time over 24h or over a 1/3/5-year term — the rate changes, the amount does not — and the annual accrual never exceeds 9,999 웃 before rolling forward.
unit.reach:
Reach as a design target

Most compensation ceilings exist to stop people getting there. This one exists to get people there. That inversion is the whole intent of the clause “enable as many people as possible to reach 9,999”, and it changes how every other number is set.

It means multiples are not a rationing device to be set as low as the treasury can defend. They are set so that a person contributing seriously for a year arrives at the ceiling. A multiple band that leaves a full-time contributor at 3,000 웃 after a year is not prudent — it is a failure of the stated goal, and it should be reported as one.

What release 35 changed here

This metric was uninterpretable until the mint went currency-free. With a wage-scaled mint, a reach rate of 0.6 in Lagos and 0.6 in Seattle described two completely different worlds, because the hours behind them differed by 47.9x. One full-time-equivalent year is now 2,080 hours everywhere, so the denominator finally means the same thing in every jurisdiction and the rate can be compared across borders without a footnote.

reach_rate  =  people who reached 9,999 in the year
               -------------------------------------
               people who contributed full-time equivalent hours

               full-time equivalent = 2,080 h    (identical in all 103 jurisdictions)

target: reach_rate -> 1.0        alert: reach_rate < 0.6

A falling reach rate means multiples have drifted below the value of the work, or that the treasury is quietly rationing through the multiple band instead of saying so. Either way it is visible in one number, published, before it becomes a grievance. And a reach rate that differs sharply between jurisdictions is now a real signal rather than an artefact of the mint — it means the work is being valued differently in different places, which is exactly the thing this framework exists to see.
coin.reach:
One Coin, Many Currencies

The ledger recognises four instruments — Seed, ♡, 웃, ◬ — and it recognises them identically whether the pod convenes in Austin, Lagos, or Manila. What changes from place to place is never the framework; it is only the number attached to a local hour. This is the discipline that lets Vision 2525 claim a genuine universality.

The anchor is the local hour itself. One 웃 base equals one hour of qualified human time valued at 1× the local minimum wage, multiplied by M for the work’s declared multiplier. In Austin, at a $7.25 statutory floor, that base hour prices in dollars. In Lagos, at Nigeria’s wage floor, the same base hour prices in naira, at a different number, for a different cost of living, without either number being converted into the other for comparison. A contributor in Lagos who earns 40 웃 in a month has not earned less than a contributor in Austin who earns 40 웃 in the same month. Each has earned forty hours of locally-anchored recognition, full stop. The system does not compute an exchange rate between them because it was never built to rank them.

Seed follows the identical rule at a smaller denomination: one seventh of a local minimum-wage hour, purchased once and renewed on the same fraction annually. Texas prices Seed at $7.25 ÷ 7 — $1.036 — plus the same amount again each year. Nigeria prices Seed at its own floor ÷ 7 — roughly $0.0486 in local-currency terms — plus the same renewal. Membership costs the same share of an hour’s work everywhere; it never costs the same number of dollars everywhere, because equal numbers across unequal economies is not fairness — it is an accident of arithmetic that happens to favour whichever economy set the number.

One coin, one rule, many prices. The formula is constant: Seed = local floor ÷ 7; 웃 base = local floor × 1; ♡ and ◬ carry no currency at all until they resolve into a 웃-denominated raise. Only the inputs move, region by region — never the equation.

This is also where the not-a-security posture does its quietest work. Nothing about a locally-priced instrument becomes tradable, transferable, or capable of appreciating: Seed does not convert between regions any more than it converts between people, and 웃 earned in one currency does not accrue value by sitting still while another region’s currency moves. There is no arbitrage to run, because there is nothing to buy low and sell high — only qualified hours, priced where they were worked, recognised where they were earned. A regulator in any jurisdiction examining the mechanism finds the same answer Austin finds and the same answer Lagos finds: recognition tracks verified human time against a public local benchmark, not speculation against a floating one.

The practical effect is a governance engine that can be piloted in one city and deployed on every continent without rewriting its mathematics — only its inputs. Austin proves the model; Lagos, Manila, and every region after them do not have to fit themselves into Austin’s currency to participate in Austin’s framework. They bring their own floor, and the coin already knows what to do with it.

— MoT
paper.s2:
§2 · THE CEILING AND THE FLOOR ↑ contents

§2   The Ceiling and the Floor

Extends §1

You already know that a year is the wrong container for a life. Somewhere behind you sits a season when you did the work of three ordinary years — a launch, a harvest, a parent nursed through an illness — and somewhere near it sits a season when you could barely lift the ordinary load. Effort arrives the way weather does, in fronts and lulls. Yet nearly every rule we live under is cut to the calendar: earn inside the year or lose it, qualify now or start over. A limit that forgets what you did last season is not neutral. It quietly teaches you never to rest — the opposite of what a limit should teach.

Here, the ceiling keeps a memory. Whatever exceeds it in one year is not clipped and discarded; it pours into the year ahead, fills that year to the same nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine, and spills onward, one year at a time, no year ever holding more, until the ninety-ninth year of a life. The arithmetic is the kind you can redo at a kitchen table: take everything you have been recognised for, divide by one year’s ceiling, and the whole-number answer is how many years are covered; the fraction left over starts the next. Division, remainder, done. No interest accrues, no early contribution multiplies, no late one is docked — because the only input is hours of a life, and hours do not breed.

See what the division guards. An extraordinary year cannot become capital; it becomes rest — the standing right to say no. A covered year is not money compounding in the dark — it is next winter, already warm. The coverage stops twice, at the edge of a lifetime and at death, because overflow that outlives its person has a name: an estate. Estates compound into dynasties within a few generations. So everything a person has secured — the covered years ahead, the ceiling arriving year by year as a livelihood rather than a lump — ends where the person ends.

And there the design tells the truth on itself. Two rules were declared beyond amendment: a payout unfolds across the years a contributor elects — one, three, or five — and nothing passes at death. Let someone die in the second year of a five-year election, and the rules give opposite orders about what is still owed. It is not smoothed over. The collision is entered in the register as open, and reserved for a deliberate human decision, not a reading that pretends the seam away. A framework meant to run for centuries earns trust here — not by having no contradictions, but by refusing to hide the one it has.

You can test this before you believe any of it. Write down your last handful of years, as heavy and light. Apply the division and watch the heavy ones reach forward to shelter the light ones — no permission required, one calculator, a quiet minute. Then turn to whichever system pays you now and ask it one question: when I give more than the year can hold, where does the excess go? If the answer is nowhere, you have found what was quietly being taken — and you now hold the arithmetic that counts it differently.

Needs

A ceiling with no memory punishes exactly the people it was built to protect. Very few lives deliver effort evenly. A carpenter works three intense seasons and a quiet one. A researcher gives four years to a problem and then needs a year to recover from it. A parent disappears from paid work for two years and returns. Any system that caps a year and discards the excess tells all of them the same thing: your uneven life is your problem. That is how well-meant limits become quiet punishments, and it is the most common way a fairness mechanism turns into its opposite without anyone deciding that it should.

Outcomes

Contribution above the ceiling is not lost and does not compound into wealth. It rolls forward, securing the next year, and the year after, bounded at age ninety-nine. Someone who contributes intensely for three years can buy quiet for four. What a person holds is not a balance that grows without them but a floor that travels with them, and the difference matters more than it sounds: a balance invites you to watch it, and a floor lets you stop watching.

Solution

Secured years are computed by division and nothing else. Cumulative recognition divided by the annual ceiling gives whole years secured; the remainder covers the following year. There is no interest, no compounding, no multiplier for having contributed early, and no penalty for having contributed late. The calculation is published, so anyone can check their own without asking permission. Bounded at ninety-nine because that is roughly the outer edge of a human life and a mechanism that extends past its subject is not a mechanism any more.

Evidence

The obvious question is what happens to someone who accrues more than a lifetime, and the honest answer is that we do not know yet, it is written in the register as unresolved, and this section will not pretend otherwise. There is a harder question underneath it that we do know about and cannot yet answer: the elected-term payout guarantee and the rule that nothing inherits cannot both hold for a person who dies inside the term. Both were declared immutable. They contradict. It is defect twenty-two, it is published, and it is waiting on a human decision rather than a clever reconciliation.
unit.carry:
The rolling floor — a good year protects the years after it

The ceiling is 9,999 웃 per natural person per year, and it is hard. What it never said is what happens to contribution above it. The answer is neither of the two obvious ones. It does not vanish, and it does not pay out faster.

The rule

Contribution above the ceiling in one year fills the following year to 9,999. Any remainder fills the year after that, and so on — forward, one year at a time, until the contributor’s ninety-ninth year. A person is not paid more. A person is secured for longer.

remainder      =  cumulative 웃 − ( secured_years × 9,999 )   → partial cover of the next year

✓ Self-limiting by construction — nobody shortcuts a lifetime

Securing every year to ninety-nine from age thirty-one means 679,932 웃. Even at the highest published band that is 67,993 hours, or 32.7 full-time years of witnessed work. The mechanism is generous and it cannot be gamed into a windfall, because the only input is time and time does not compress.

unit.death:
Nothing inherits

Every system that pays people eventually faces the same question: what happens when a contributor dies?

Answer with inheritance and you have built a dynasty engine.The second generation holds what the first earned. The third holds what neither earned. Within four generations the framework is precisely the concentrated actor every other page of it was designed to resist.
The rule · class: Immutable

웃 ends with the person who earned it. No transfer on death, no beneficiary designation, no assignment, no trust instrument, no probate claim. Reserved forward years extinguish with the rest. A lump sum accrued without work is never available to anyone, at any point, by any route.

What extinction actually does

at death: cumulative 웃 → 0 reserved forward years → 0 committed reserve → falls by the extinguished amount headroom → rises by the same amount no trustee · no probate · no discretion · nothing to litigate
The scale of it, stated plainly

A contributor who had secured ten years and part of an eleventh holds 104,000 웃. At the Austin anchor that is $754,000.00 of committed reserve, and at death all of it returns to fund other people’s security. The framework does not keep it. It re-commits it.

What passes instead — an invitation, not a bequest

Every immediate family member may purchase one Seed Token, permanently linked to the person who died. As many as that person actually had; there is no cap. Note the direction: they pay in. Nothing is paid out.

What the family receivesWhat the family does not receive
The right — never the obligation — to purchase one token each, at 1/7 of a local minimum-wage hour: 8m 34s of work, the same slice everyone else pays.Any 웃. Any settlement. Any instalment. Any claim of any kind.
A permanent memorial link on the record: this token stands beside that contributor’s work.Governance weight. A Seed Token confers none, for them as for everyone.
The same standing every funder has, and not one degree more.Preference, priority, or any better term than a stranger would get.
At the Austin anchor a token is exactly 1.00. Eight family members paying in is 8.00 against 754,000 released — 94,250 to one, inward. Forty is 40.00, and still 18,850 to one. The direction survives an order of magnitude, which is how you can tell the old cap of ten was never doing the work that sentence credited it with.
Say it in one sentence, because it will be misread

They do not inherit worth. They receive an option to join. Not a payout, not a transfer, not a discount, not a place in a queue — an option to buy, in their own year, at their own local price, the identical instrument any stranger may buy on the identical terms.

The smallness is deliberate. A framework that gave a grieving family more than society gets would begin building the very dynasty engine this section exists to prevent. What passes to them is a name on the record beside the person who earned it, and the same door everyone else walks through.

Why the cap had to go

⚠ Release 46 argued against itself, and we did not notice

That release promised, in its own words, that “a family is never asked to rank itself or to choose which relationships qualify” — and then, two sentences later, said “where more than ten are eligible, the family decides among themselves.”

Under a cap, a family with eleven eligible people IS asked to rank itself, at the worst possible moment, over a dollar. Removing the cap is the only way the promise and the mechanism agree. The earlier wording stays readable at release 46.

Who counts as immediate family

The definition follows the United States federal standard for bereavement and survivor benefits — a published, checkable list: spouse or domestic partner; children, including step, adopted and foster; parents, including step; siblings, including step and half; grandparents; grandchildren; and parents-in-law. Bounded by biology and law rather than by a number we chose, which is a better limit precisely because nobody has to enforce it and nobody has to argue about it.

Two properties that matter more than a cap ever did

Nobody ranks anybody. The framework never adjudicates a family list, because with no cap there is nothing left to adjudicate. And election is free: any eligible person may decline, and declining costs them nothing and costs the family nothing.

One standard: the United States definition, with Texas applied wherever Texas is more favorable. The framework does not adopt regional equivalents. The American bereavement and survivor standard is the operating definition everywhere the framework runs, and the Texas standard governs wherever it treats the person better. It moves only one way: if we the people elect, together, to seat the framework in another country, that country’s standard is adopted by the same vote — never by an administrator’s discretion. Fixed reference, Immutable obligation — chosen as one people, changed only as one people.

⚠ The consequence, stated rather than buried

A Seed Token carries a bounded return-of-buy-in claim at shutdown (§7), not a claim on reserves broadly, so removing the cap admits marginally more claimants. The dilution is bounded by real family sizes rather than by ambition, and each token claims only the increase between its purchase year and the shutdown year. We prefer a negligible dilution to making a grieving family choose which of its members counts. Disagree with that trade if you like — it is written down so you can.

⚠ Defect 22 — two locked terms collide, and this does not decide between them

A contributor two years into an elected five-year entitlement has three further years of the ceiling already earned and not yet drawn — three times $72,492.75 at the Austin anchor. Two Immutable rules reach for it. The election narrows the window — a one-year term closes most of it — but the three- and five-year elections still cross it, so the contradiction stands until the human decision is made.

“Paid out over the elected term, guaranteed” says those instalments are owed. “Nothing inherits” says nothing survives the person. Both are locked. They cannot both hold.

The reading I would take, and it is not mine to settle: the guarantee is a promise to a person, protecting them against next year — not a promise to an estate, protecting it against their death. On that reading outstanding instalments extinguish with everything else, and the Seed Token right replaces them. That narrows a locked term, which must be ratified rather than assumed. Open for the operator.

What makes this bearable is what it becomes. A family that cannot be paid can still be counted — permanently, publicly, beside the person they lost, for eight and a half minutes of work each. An ending turns into a beginning, which is the only honest thing an ending can become in a framework built to run for five hundred years.
unit.payout:
Real time, or over one, three, or five years — the contributor’s election, guaranteed: the salary floor

Earned value is paid as the contributor elects — in real time, streamed at a dollars-per-minute rate as it is earned, up to the 9,999 웃/yr maximum rate, with any excess rolling forward; or over a term of one, three, or five years, funded by a ring-fenced reserve whose balance is published monthly. The guarantee is structural, not aspirational, and the election belongs to the contributor alone — five years is the default where none is made. A shorter term is the same money sooner; the reserve funds every committed instalment whichever election is chosen, so the coverage inequality binds identically. The purpose is stated in the locked definition: livelihood security and continuity, not lump-sum wealth.

A contributor may accrue up to five times a single year’s ceiling. What that buys is not a bigger payment — the ceiling is the ceiling — it is the elected term of it: the full annual figure this year and, at the five-year election, in each of the next four, whether or not another hour is ever contributed. The filling rule is the whole mechanism and it is one sentence: a year fills to 9999 웃 and no further, and the excess flows forward into the next year, which is also capped at 9999 웃. At the five-year election, five years of that is the reach of a single year’s contribution; anything still unspent flows into year six on the same rule. No year ever pays more than 9999 웃, and nothing is ever lost — it waits. The figure is chosen rather than derived: 9999 웃 settles in Texas at $72,492.75, which is a reasonable salary there and a long way above the poverty line. That is what the unit was always for.
