Each annual figure IS the ceiling settled at the local rate — not a fifth of it. Five years of accrual buys five years of the same figure at the longest election, and year six holds whatever was earned beyond that. The local numbers differ because the local floors differ; the slice of a life is identical everywhere.

Two properties follow, and both are the point rather than side effects.

It is a floor, not a windfall. A contributor at the ceiling knows what the next four years hold even if they never contribute again. That is what “continuity” means in the locked definition, and it is the difference between being paid and being secure.

It is an accruing balance, not a sum anybody hands over. The figures above are annual CAPS on what may be drawn, not cheques that arrive on a date. Recognition accrues continuously as $/min into escrow against the ring-fenced reserve; the real-time election draws that balance as it fills — the shape of a driver taking instant pay several times a day rather than waiting for Friday — while an elected term spreads the same balance over guaranteed instalments. The ceiling governs the year; the timing belongs to the person.

It converts recognition into stability instead of into leverage. Five times $72,492.75 arriving at once is capital, and capital seeks influence. The same accrual drawn against an annual ceiling is a salary. The ceiling stops accumulation across people; the elected horizon — at most five years — stops it across time; and the annual cap stops a large balance becoming a large payment.

⚠ The cost of the guarantee

The word guaranteed is doing enormous work here, and it is the most legally dangerous word in the document. A guaranteed multi-year payment stream to individuals is, in substance, a defined-benefit obligation. It is treated as a first-order legal problem later in this document rather than as a footnote, because it is the clause a regulator reaches for first.
unit.tranche:
The two tranches — wage floor and acceleration

Draws against pre-funded escrow are always trailing, never advanced: a contributor withdraws only against 웃 already accrued for hours Measurement of Time has independently logged. This block is the single definition of the split; the ceiling and the accelerator both read it.

One split, defined once

Each accrual splits automatically into two tranches. The Wage-Floor Tranche is hours at the greater of the eXeL 1/7-hour reference and the local statutory minimum — available immediately through the Uber-style draw and never clawed back, for it is wages for verified hours, owed regardless of outcome. The Acceleration Tranche is everything the multiple M adds above that floor — the ◬ recognition premium — which remains locked in escrow until independently witnessed.

The Acceleration Tranche releases progressively as the task clears each De-Risk Gateway stage — Pilot, Refine, Qualify, Adopt — with final release gated on Governance and Quote Board sign-off confirming the acceleration evidence against its frozen baseline. Should the outcome fail to qualify, the Wage-Floor already drawn is never seized, while any undrawn Acceleration reverts to escrow as a new, append-only entry.

The only carve-out

Fraudulently logged hours are the sole exception: voided going forward and referred to governance, never a retroactive seizure of legitimate pay. Because the split happens before currency conversion, the 9,999 ceiling bites at the same real contribution in every region (D2).
human.story:
What year five means

Everything above is machinery. Here is what the machinery is for.

Adaeze is thirty-one and lives outside Lagos. She has a degree she could not afford to finish on time and a talent for finding the failure in a process before it fails. In the first year she contributes nine hundred hours to a water-infrastructure programme — evenings, mostly, and the parts of Saturdays that are hers. Her contributions are assessed at six times the local minimum wage, because what she does is scarce and the band for it is published in advance.

Nine hundred hours at six times is 5,400 웃. She has not reached the ceiling. She has earned a settlement of about $1,836 in her own currency, arriving over the term she elects: all of it in one year, about $612 a year over three, or roughly $367 a year over five.

That is not a life-changing number and this document will not pretend otherwise. Here is what it is.

It is hers, permanently, and it does not depend on anyone remembering her. The record is not a reference she must ask a manager for. It says what she contributed, to which programme, assessed in which band, and what came of it — and it will still say that when the programme is finished and the people who ran it have moved on.

In her second year she reaches the ceiling. In the third, and the fourth. By year five, the instalments from five overlapping cohorts have stacked, and the floor beneath her is the full ceiling value, arriving whether or not she contributes anything that year.

That is the whole design in one person. Not a windfall — a windfall would have been spent or taken. A floor. She can now refuse work that is beneath her, take the month her mother is ill, or contribute to something that will not pay for three years, because next year is already underwritten.

The ceiling is not what protects her from other people. The election is what protects her: five years if she wants next year already covered, one if she needs the money now.Why the payout schedule is in the locked definition, and not in a policy that could be revised

And in Austin, someone doing comparable work at a comparable band earns the same 5,400 웃 and settles at $39,150, because that is what a comparable floor costs in Texas. Same recognition. Same ceiling. Same election. Different money, because money is local and dignity is not.
hi.floor.dignity:
What arrives today, and what waits to be believed

Marisol logs an hour in Austin at nine in the morning. Chidinma logs one in Lagos at two in the afternoon, her time. Ligaya logs one in Manila past midnight, because the client she is helping keeps European hours. None of them know each other, and none of them need to. What binds them is smaller than a shared employer and larger than a shared currency: the same rule decided, in advance, what each of their hours would become the moment it was logged.

Say the task each of them completes is ordinary — a report tightened, a dataset cleaned, a translation checked against a frozen baseline — and say, this time, no acceleration has yet been shown. Each earns one 웃 for the hour itself, with no multiple attached, because the multiple is never assumed; it is only ever confirmed, later, against evidence a pod can point to. That single 웃 is the whole of the Wage-Floor Tranche, and it draws the same day, in the currency each of them actually spends: Marisol’s rent money, Chidinma’s market money, Ligaya’s fare money home. None of the three had to persuade anyone that their hour mattered. It already had.

Now say a second hour, logged by any one of them on a harder task, where the tool did real work and the multiple looks, provisionally, like two or three. Those extra 웃 do not draw the same day. They sit in escrow, because a multiple is a claim about acceleration, and a claim is not yet evidence — it becomes evidence when an independent pod checks the deliverable against the baseline and the De-Risk Gateway lets the work through its stages, one confirmation at a time. This is not distrust of Marisol, Chidinma, or Ligaya. It is the opposite of distrust: it is the system refusing to let anyone, including itself, mint recognition on a hope. The floor never asks to be believed. The ceiling above it always does.

Sit with what this buys each of them, separately. It buys Chidinma the ability to plan a week on wages that cannot be revoked by a gate she does not control, even while a larger number waits on the far side of that gate. It buys Ligaya the right to decline a rushed sign-off she is not confident in, because nothing about her rent depends on the acceleration clearing on anyone else’s schedule. It buys Marisol the same certainty at a larger figure, because her region’s floor is larger — not because she is owed more trust, but because her groceries cost more. The floor is not generosity. It is wages for hours already worked, and wages for hours already worked are not something one human should be asked to gamble with on another human’s behalf.

That is the entire moral weight of the split, stated without the arithmetic: nobody should have to choose between eating this week and being honest about how fast the tool actually worked. Separate the floor from the acceleration and nobody has to. The hour was real either way, and the money for the hour that was real arrives whether or not the story about the tool turns out, on inspection, to be true. Three cities, three currencies, one rule that never once asked where any of them were born.

— MoT
paper.s3:
§3 · THE WALL ↑ contents

§3   The Wall

Extends §1

You have sat in the room this section was built for. A tenants meeting, a parish hall, a co-op board — the agenda promised everyone present would decide together. But one chair held the person who paid for the study, another held the consultant whose proposal arrived already written, and by the time hands went up the answer had a shape nobody voted on. And still you walked home knowing your voice had weighed less than somebody’s chequebook. That is the injury this section answers: theft without a thief — until someone treated it as architecture instead of crime.

The repair begins with a distinction most systems never draw. Two questions hide inside the word decide. Which good work deserves attention first is a question effort and generosity may fairly lean on; whether the work happens at all, who leads it, when it must stop — those belong to persons simply because they are persons. Collapse the two onto one ballot and everything a supporter gives becomes, quietly, a lever on everything else. Separate them, give each its own arithmetic, and money keeps its honest role while losing its dishonest one.

So the ordering side speaks in square roots: influence rises only as the square root of hours given — four times the hours buys twice the say, a hundred times buys only ten — and above that a ceiling of fifteen per cent, reasserted every round, hands whatever overflows back to everyone else. The sovereign side speaks the plainest arithmetic there is: each verified human counts once, and nothing else counts at all. The sovereign tally was not fitted with a guard against wealth; it was built with no place for wealth to enter. No field to fill, no weight to inflate, no rule a tired administrator might one day forget to apply. An absence asks nothing of anyone, and sells nothing to anyone.

Now the honest part. Walls are not tested by the powerless; the powerless were never the threat. It will be tested by the resourceful and the sincere — the foundation with conditions folded into its kindness, the agency whose help arrives holding a steering wheel, the ally who assumed devotion had earned a little authority. The pressure will sound like generosity, because it will be generosity. The wall earns its existence on the day a major funder learns that funding bought a public record of thanks and nothing more — and either stays, which proves the mission mattered, or leaves, which proves what actually did. One more honesty: today only the ordering half stands as running, tested code; the sovereign half remains a commitment on paper, and the open register beneath this page says so, along with the place where present code still leans on the wall it should stand clear of. A structure that hid its own gaps would be a procedure wearing a costume.

You do not need this framework to use its test. In the next room where something is decided, ask two questions: which kind of question is on the table, and whether the same instrument — the same money, the same title, the same credit — is answering both. Wherever one instrument answers both, you have found the crack before the water has. What you do about it is yours.

Needs

Money finds its way into governance the way water finds a crack. It does not need anyone corrupt to do it. It arrives through consultation budgets, through who can afford to attend, through which analysis gets commissioned, through whose proposal is already drafted when the meeting starts. Every one of those doors was left open by someone acting reasonably. That is why systems designed to keep money out of decisions almost always fail: they defend against bad actors, and the actual mechanism runs entirely on good ones.

Outcomes

There is a line in this framework that money can reach and cannot cross. It is drawn structurally rather than defended procedurally. Contribution can shape which problems get attention. It cannot shape who is permitted to say so. A funder and a person who has never given a cent hold exactly the same weight on the question of whether something should exist at all, and no amount of either money or accumulated recognition changes that ratio by any margin.

Solution

Sovereign questions run on one person, one vote, unweighted and uncapped: whether to do something, whether to stop, whether to switch the system off. Prioritisation, the ordering of work already agreed on, runs on quadratic weighting with an iterative fifteen per cent influence cap and redistribution, so concentration is bled off in every round rather than tolerated. Every path money can travel terminates on the prioritisation side. It shapes a queue. It cannot decide the queue exists.

Evidence

This is the claim on which everything else either holds or fails, and it is the one most easily tested. It is running code rather than intention. Quadratic ranking with cap and redistribution is implemented and covered by one hundred and sixty-four tests. The unweighted sovereign path takes no recognition input at all, which is not a rule enforced somewhere but a value the function never receives. You cannot damp an input that was never wired. Where a defence can be structural rather than procedural, we have made it structural, because procedures require somebody to keep following them and structures do not.
gov.wall:
Sovereignty is not prioritisation

This is the finding everything else in this document follows from, and it should have been here from release 1.

Most governance systems collapse two different questions onto one ballot: what should we do? and who decides? They are not the same question and they must not share a weighting rule.

SovereigntyPrioritisation
DecidesWho leads · amendments · purpose · removal · dissolutionWhich themes rank · what gets built first · sequencing
WeightingNone. One verified person, one vote.Quadratic on contributed time, capped at 15% influence.
Money may enterNever. By any route, direct or laundered through contribution.Never either — though funding capacity legitimately shapes what is feasible.
Status todayProposed — no unweighted sovereignty ballot exists in codeImplemented cube7_ranking/ranking_aggregation.py:32-43
Prioritisation is already built and already resistant to plutocracy. Sovereignty is not yet built — which is fortunate, because building it with the wrong weighting rule would be far harder to undo than building it right.

The prioritisation half is real code. _quadratic_weights computes sqrt(tokens_staked), normalises to 1.0, then applies an iterative 15% influence cap with redistribution. Quadratic weighting lets a person express intensity — caring twice as much costs four times as much — while making domination arithmetically expensive. The cap makes it impossible outright.
gov.layers:
The three-layer separation

Capture happens where two rights ride on the same instrument. If the thing that records your contribution is also the thing that pays you and also the thing that votes, then buying one buys all three. The remedy is to make them different instruments by construction.

ParticipationVerified personhood — one SeedAttestation of being one natural person.The sovereignty vote. Standing to propose. Standing to be elected.No economic right whatsoever. It cannot be sold because it is not property.
FundingContribution receipt — inertGiving money.A permanent public record that you funded the work, and traceability of where it went.No vote. No weight. No token. No claim. Non-transferable.
Three layers, three instruments, no overlap. The funding receipt is deliberately inert: worthless to anyone seeking influence, meaningful to anyone seeking to be counted.

This is not novel policy invented here. It is what the Atlantis Accords already commit to, in language that leaves no room: “No contribution buys governance influence, from any source, ever.” The separation is the enforcement mechanism for a promise already made.

And it is breached in code today — see defect 1 in the register.
gov.primacy:
Human Primacy of Power

Article · class: Immutable

No entity — corporate, governmental, algorithmic, or aggregated — shall hold governing authority exceeding that of one natural person. Authority is a property of persons. It may be exercised on behalf of an organisation, but it is never held by one, never accumulated across one, and never inherited by an instrument.

The article closes the aggregation loophole that defeats most one-person-one-vote schemes: an organisation cannot vote, but nothing stops it directing a thousand people who can. Under Human Primacy, an organisation’s disclosed influence is bounded by one regardless of how many affiliated persons it has, and undisclosed direction of votes is itself the violation. Enforcement is not perfect — no scheme’s is — but it makes the attack expensive, detectable and nameable, which is the realistic bar.

gov.aidoor:
The Adaptive AI-Authority Door

Evidence earns an AI agent a wider mandate to execute; it never earns the agent a vote, a signature, or a claim. Authority here widens by delegation, not by dissolution of the human boundary.

Three states
  • Advisory — the default and the ceiling for any agent with no witnessed record: it may propose, draft, flag and simulate, and nothing it produces has independent effect.
  • Bounded-Autonomous — a human-authored, Council-ratified, capped and reversible envelope, for example scheduled escrow withdrawals inside the thresholds already fixed by D3, which a witnessed accuracy record against a frozen baseline may widen, and which any single verified miss immediately narrows.
  • Sovereign — the sovereignty vote, the signature, the settlement claim — permanently closed to every machine agent, under Human Primacy of Power, regardless of accuracy, tenure, or accumulated acceleration evidence.
Widens by delegation, not dissolution

A human signs the mandate’s boundary once, the agent executes inside it, and the rule that live execution always requires human authority is satisfied at the moment of that signature, not bypassed by what follows. Every bounded action carries the ledger attribution of its human operator of record, who remains liable. Grant is slow and Council-gated; revocation is immediate and needs no majority. Irreversible or unbounded actions — disbursement above the escrow threshold, anything touching a sovereignty vote or signature — are structurally excluded, not merely gated higher.
paper.s4:
§4 · THE SHIELD ↑ contents

§4   The Shield

Extends §1

The deepest safety you have ever felt did not come from a guard. It came from absence. Nobody stands watch over the air, because nobody can carry the air away. Everything else you love is kept by vigilance — a tax paid in attention, and attention runs out, and you sleep. Thought Mastery, inside a person, is the practice of refusing a temptation before it ripens into an act. Inside an institution the same refusal must be poured into structure, because an institution does not sleep once; it sleeps forever, one retirement at a time.

Do the multiplication yourself. A hostile offer is a price multiplied by a count of shares. Set the count to zero and the offer, at any price, buys nothing — not because a court weighed it, but because multiplication did. When the only lawful destination for value is another locked purpose, money can travel and purpose cannot. A guarantee collapses the day obligations exceed holdings; let no obligation arise except against holdings already present, and the fatal inequality becomes unreachable. Each defence is a subtraction performed once, and what was subtracted can no longer be seized or inherited.

Then count jurisdictions. One incorporation is one courtroom, one statute, one signature on one bad afternoon — a single point of failure wearing a flag. A separate legal body under each region’s own law turns shutdown into a coincidence: every government must act simultaneously, and independent chances multiply, so the odds of all falling together shrink below the odds of any one. Notice which way the shield faces: the entity exists to be the thing a plaintiff can name, so that a human being never has to be. And measure the design at its weakest point — an opponent picks the venue, so the only protection that counts is what still stands in the least sympathetic courtroom.

The part this page must say plainly, because the tables beneath it cannot. Shields fail. They fail more often than on paper: most asset locks in history were not broken but quietly reinterpreted by the people they inconvenienced, through amendment powers everyone assumed were decorative. The paper holds; the meaning leaks. A funded reserve is only as honest as the currency holding it. Five subtractions close five named routes of capture, and the set of routes is not closed; nobody can subtract what has not been invented yet. What survives that admission is smaller and harder than a certainty: a collapse that would need many independent hands, in many countries, over a long time — and a reader in each generation who can recompute why every zero sits where it sits.

Take the test with you; it needs one afternoon and nobody’s blessing. Pick any institution your life leans on and ask four questions. What does it own that a buyer could want? Who could sell it? Which single signature could end it? Are its promises backed by holdings it has, or holdings it hopes for? Where the answers frighten you, you have found the shape of the next capture before it dresses itself as good sense. Keep the quietest clause: the same absence that keeps anyone from owning this keeps it from owning you. You may leave whole, at any hour — and whether you stay was always yours.

Needs

Anything worth building eventually becomes worth capturing, and the capture rarely looks like theft. It looks like an acquisition everyone agrees is sensible, a jurisdiction offering better terms, a governance simplification that removes a veto nobody had used recently. You have seen this happen to something you cared about. Almost everyone has, and history does not lack for organisations founded on principle and ended by paperwork.

The usual defence is a promise: charters, mission statements, boards that pledge to hold the line. Promises are only as durable as the people holding them — and five hundred years is longer than any person, any board, or almost any country. The wall in the last section kept money out of the vote. This section is about the quieter danger: us.

Outcomes

Five defences that require nobody to stay honest. Not because we assume bad faith, but because a structure that depends on good faith has quietly delegated its survival to strangers who are not born yet — to you, if you are reading this a century from now, and to people you will never meet.

What cannot be acquired cannot be lost in an acquisition. What was never distributable cannot be distributed under pressure. Read that pair twice: it is the entire logic of the shield, and it protects you without asking you to trust us.

Solution

So here is the renunciation, written to you, in advance, and binding: no equity exists, so there is nothing to buy — the most common capture route is closed by absence rather than by rule. Assets are locked against distribution. Legal personality is federated and domestic, so no single jurisdiction holds the whole and no single court can reach it. Recognition can never be purchased at any price. Reserves are funded rather than pledged, because a pledge is a promise wearing a balance sheet.

No supervoting class. No founder allocation. No reserved seat. No perpetual role. We give these up while we are the ones who would benefit from keeping them, because a renunciation made after the temptation arrives is a negotiation. The list is locked at five: a sixth instrument, if ever proposed, must arrive the way these five did — priced, its cost stated in the unit it will actually be paid in — or it does not join.

Evidence

Each refusal cost something specific, and pretending otherwise would make this list a sales pitch. Refusing investor capital cost speed, measured in orders of magnitude. Refusing transferable recognition cost liquidity — and with it every person who would have participated only if they could sell later. Refusing a single incorporation cost legal simplicity and the ability to answer basic questions in one sentence. Refusing inheritance cost the most emotionally reasonable request families make, and that one still hurts to defend.

What every refusal bought was the same thing: nothing to acquire, therefore nothing to capture. If you believe one of those trades was wrong, you now hold enough detail to build the other version yourself — which is the honest outcome of publishing a cost rather than a claim, and an invitation rather than a dare. One threat stays open because honesty requires it: the patient opponent who accepts every rule and simply outwaits the people who understood why the rules exist. No structure closes that — only the record, and the readers it keeps making.
legal.doctrine:
The non-stoppability doctrine

The question this section answers is narrow and practical: what would it take for a government to stop this, and what can be built now so that the answer is “more than it is worth”?

The instinct is to argue better. That is the wrong instinct, because an argument can be lost and a structure cannot be out-argued. The doctrine here is different:

Defensibility comes from what the framework permanently gives up, not from what it claims.The organising principle of the entire legal design

Every renunciation removes an attack line and a regulator at the same time. That inverts the usual posture: instead of defending against a critic, the structure makes the critic’s argument unavailable. There is no counter-argument to “there are no shares”.

Three things follow, and they are what the rest of this part builds:

Nothing to acquire
No equity, no shares, no tradeable claim. An entity with nothing to buy cannot be bought, raided, or taken over.
Nothing to extract
An asset lock: value can only ever move to another purpose-locked body, never to individuals. This is what makes “they will enrich themselves” false rather than merely denied.
Nothing to switch off
A domestic legal person in each participating region rather than one foreign entity soliciting inward. No single government holds an off switch, and no region is funded from abroad.
legal.shields:
The Five Shields

Each shield is a structural property rather than a policy position, which is what makes it hold when nobody is defending it.

#ShieldWhat it defeatsClass
INo equity, everAcquisition, hostile takeover, accumulation of control by capital. There is no instrument to accumulate.Immutable
IIAsset lockExtraction, self-dealing, private benefit. Assets may only transfer to another purpose-locked body, including on dissolution.Immutable
IIIFederated domestic personalitySingle-government shutdown, foreign-influence designation, cross-border solicitation restrictions. Each region hosts its own legal person under its own law.Immutable
IVRecognition is never purchasableThe investment-of-money limb of the securities analysis, and the “the rich buy influence” attack, in one move.Immutable
VFunded reserveInsolvency of a guaranteed obligation — the single most likely trigger for regulatory intervention. Obligations may only be incurred against reserves actually held.Immutable
All five are Immutable by design. A shield that can be amended by the body it constrains is not a shield; it is a preference.

Shields I to IV were implicit in the Atlantis Accords and are made explicit here. Shield V is new, and it exists because the guaranteed payout election (one, three, or five years) makes it necessary — see the section on the guarantee exposure below.
legal.renounce:
The renunciation table

Read the middle column as the speech a hostile politician would give. Each line is unavailable to them — not because it has been rebutted, but because the thing it attacks does not exist.

Permanently renouncedThe attack it foreclosesThe regulator it removes
No equity. No shares. Ever.“An investment fund will end up owning this.”Takeover and control regimes — nothing to acquire.

legal.entity:
The legal form

The vehicle that carries the Five Shields is a steward-ownership, asset-locked purpose entity, federated as a domestic legal person in each participating region. Its four properties map one to one onto the shields:

No equity
Shield I. Nothing to acquire; no shares exist to be bought or inherited.
Asset lock
Shield II. Assets transfer only to another purpose-locked body — a statutory feature of several existing community-interest forms rather than a contractual promise.
Control separated from capital
Shield IV. Economic rights and governance rights are different instruments by construction, so acquiring one cannot acquire the other.
Federated personality
Shield III. Each region hosts its own legal person, so no government holds a global off switch and no region is funded from abroad.

Real precedents exist and none of them are exotic: industrial foundations holding operating companies in perpetuity, statutory asset-locked community forms, and non-distributing purpose trusts. They are offered here as patterns with trade-offs, not as a recommendation of one vehicle. Each carries materially different tax, reporting and dissolution consequences in each jurisdiction, and the right answer in Delaware is the wrong answer in Mumbai. Requires qualified local counsel in every region, without exception.
paper.s5:
§5 · THE LEDGER ↑ contents

§5   The Ledger

Extends §1

Every person keeps two pasts: the one that happened and the one you tell, and the second is under maintenance every time you revisit it — softened and justified until only the flattering account survives. You know this because a few memories refuse the treatment: a sentence spoken in anger that stays exactly worded. That refusal is the part of you that will not let comfort overwrite evidence, and why you trust those memories and merely enjoy the rest. An institution has no such part unless one is built deliberately. Left alone, it remembers the way flattery remembers.

The machinery built here is blunt. Nothing written is ever unwritten. A correction never replaces its error; it is laid down after it, carrying the reason recorded at the moment of writing, not assembled later by whoever needs the story to end well. To see any earlier state, run one small rule: walk the entries in order, keep the newest that existed then, print what you kept. The rule consults no clock and no person — a reconstruction that needs a person is a reconstruction that person can refuse, delay, or improve.

The proof is nothing but comparison — the only arithmetic honesty requires: equal or not equal, and no adjective improves either answer. Each published state is rebuilt thirty-three times and the outputs laid side by side, where one differing byte would end the claim. When the engine beneath was accelerated thirteen-fold, the speed itself went on trial: all one hundred and forty-seven published fingerprints were computed under both, and the count of tolerated differences was zero. That is a subtraction, not an assurance, and you can perform it the day you stop believing us.

Now the bill, without perfume. A past nobody can erase is a past nobody can be released from. The wrong early claim stays legible forever, and a reader arriving in bad faith can drag the view backward and hold your worst version to the light — the permanence that disciplines an institution also arms its prosecutors. Two defenses exist. An error is never the last word: its repair stands welded after it. And scope: this ledger holds claims a document chose to publish, not the movements of a life. Pointed at published claims, permanence is accountability; pointed at persons, the identical machinery is a dossier no apology can amend, and keepers of dossiers do not rot more slowly for being sincere. The line between them is a decision about what deserves to be unforgettable, made before the first entry, because afterwards there is nothing to delete with.

None of this waits for permission. Today, in a browser you own, pull the control backward and watch an earlier, mistaken wording return untouched, its correction filed behind it — the one test of our honesty we cannot pass on your behalf. Then carry the discipline to paper: one record you only ever add to. Cross nothing out; when you change your mind, write the new mind beneath the old with a line saying why. Within a season you will own something almost nobody owns — evidence about yourself that you did not curate. The next time your memory offers to improve a past you lived, you will have somewhere to check, and the checking will be yours alone.

Needs

A document that can be edited quietly is not evidence. It is a claim about the present, made by whoever holds the keys, and its reliability is exactly the reliability of that person on that day. Most institutional records are like this and almost nobody notices, because the edit that matters is never announced. Reports get updated. Figures get restated. The version you read is the version that survived, and the versions that did not survive were usually the interesting ones.

Outcomes

Every release of this document can be reconstructed by anyone, including the releases that were wrong. Move the control backwards and the earlier wording returns exactly as it was, with the mistake intact and the correction visible as a later entry rather than as a silent replacement. Nobody has to trust that we did not tamper with it. They can check, in their own browser, without asking.

Solution

The document is not stored. It is an append-only ledger of block edits, and selecting a release runs a pure function over that ledger: same release, same order, same bytes, with no clock, no randomness and no hidden state. There is no delete operation, so a superseded block stays readable rather than disappearing. Every entry carries the reason it was made, recorded at the time it was made rather than reconstructed afterwards by someone with an interest in the story.

Evidence

You are reading the output of the mechanism this section describes, which is the only honest way to introduce it. The proof runs in the page: every release replayed thirty-three times, from the ledger, with the memo bypassed, because a cache that answers the question does the same thing as no proof at all. There is a harder point buried in that detail. When the engine was made thirteen times faster, the optimisation had to be shown not to change a single published hash, and all one hundred and forty-seven were compared before and after. Speed is allowed to change. The record is not, and the difference between those two is checked by a machine rather than asserted by us.
rcore.ledger:
How this document is built

You are reading the output of the mechanism this section describes, which is the only honest way to introduce it.

Nothing above was stored as a finished page. The document is an append-only ledger of block edits, and selecting a release runs a pure function over it:

render(v, order):
    for each block id in order:
        take the newest ledger entry e where e.id == id and e.v <= v
        if one exists, emit it

same v, same order  ->  same bytes out.  always.  no clock, no randomness, no hidden state.

Three properties follow, and each of them is a governance property rather than a technical one.

Nothing is overwritten. A superseded block stays in the ledger and stays readable. Move the slider back and the earlier wording returns exactly as it was. There is no version of this document in which an inconvenient earlier claim quietly disappears.

Every change carries its cause. Each ledger entry records why it was made and which review produced it. The provenance table below is not a changelog written afterwards — it is the source the document is generated from.

Anyone can verify the reconstruction. Not by trusting a hash we publish, but by re-running it. The buttons at the foot of this page do exactly that.

A view is an order, and an order can be younger than the record

Each way of reading this document is nothing but a list of block ids handed to the same function — which is what makes a new way of reading cheap: it changes no engine, adds no second copy, and inherits the determinism guarantee whole.

It also creates a situation that has to be answered honestly. A list of ids written at release 41 names nothing that existed at release 20. Replay it there and it returns an empty document — not because the record is missing, but because that way of reading it had not been invented yet.

The rule

When the open view has nothing to show at the selected release, the reader is given the complete record for that release — which exists from release 1 — together with a plain statement of which view was asked for, when it was first written, and why it is not shown. Nothing is generated to fill the gap. A document that would rather show you the wrong thing than admit a gap has already lost the only property that makes it worth replaying.

What changed between two releases is a property of the record, not of the way you are holding it. Comparison and key improvements therefore read the complete record in every view, so two readers looking at different views of the same two releases are told the same thing about what changed.

This is R-CORE at document scale. The same discipline governs the ranking pipeline, the theming pipeline and the financial engine — where 578 of 578 assertions returned identical results across 33 independent runs, with per-unit rows reconciling exactly to their company total. The claim in this document is smaller and of exactly the same kind.
rcore.modes:
Who may append

A replayable ledger is only as trustworthy as the rule about who may add to it. That rule is not invented here; it is the execution-mode ladder that already governs every other write in the system (backend/app/core/rcore/execution_modes.py). Implemented

Seven modes exist. The same operation runs in every one of them — only the approver changes, never the underlying logic. Two guardrails are load-bearing for everything this document claims about human authority:

DEFAULT_MAX_RISK       = 0.30   # above this, no automated acceptance
DEFAULT_MIN_CONFIDENCE = 0.70   # below this, no automated acceptance

live  ->  ALWAYS requires human authority.  A permanent gate.

That last line is Human Primacy of Power expressed as executable code rather than as a principle. It is currently the only place in the entire system where the principle is enforced by a machine instead of by an intention, which is both encouraging and an honest measure of how much of this framework remains to be built.

Applied to this document: a proposed edit runs in sandbox against a copy of the ledger and can be replayed and compared. Appending it to the real ledger is a live operation, and a person signs it. The machine may draft; only a person may adopt.
rcore.spiral:
Thirty-three transitions, forward and backward

Proving the engine has no hidden state is not the same as proving the document improved. These are two different instruments.

The proof above replays one release thirty-three times and shows the thirty-three reads are identical. That is a determinism proof: nothing in the reconstruction depends on a clock, a random number, or state left behind by a previous read. It is necessary and it is not sufficient. A document can be perfectly deterministic and getting steadily worse.

What a spiral test is, and what it is for

A spiral test measures a transition rather than a release. For each pair of consecutive releases it runs the propagation in both directions:

Forward — does the newer release carry more than the older one? Blocks, words and numbered sections must rise or hold.

Backward — does the older release still replay exactly as it did before its successor existed? Same blocks, same words, same state hash. Append-only is a claim about the past, and this is the measurement that either substantiates it or does not.

The rule, written down before the results

KindWhat is measuredHow it is judged
Hard floor333 words minimum per section · exactly 19 outline entries at 111 words · 20% duplication ceilingAbsolute. The current release must be clean, and any historical breach must be closed by a named release and carry a defect number.
Directionalblocks · words · numbered sectionsMust not fall — unless the release’s own directive says it removed something. A framework may shrink. It may not shrink silently.
Envelopeshortest section · worst duplicationJudged against the floor and the ceiling, not against the previous release. Moving a section from 365 to 343 words is editing, not decay.
The third row is where the first version of this instrument was wrong: it scored every movement as a regression, which would have forbidden ever rewriting a sentence. Recorded here rather than quietly relaxed.

What the thirty-three transitions found

forward   improved, held, or the reduction is recorded   33/33
floors    333 words · 19 outline entries · 20% duplication  33/33
backward  earlier release replays byte-identical afterwards  33/33

latest    shortest section 343 · outline 19/19 · duplication 7.1%
⚠ And it found this, which is why it exists

The white paper was written by restating the record in a new voice, and for thirteen releases it breached our own 20% duplication ceiling — worst case 71.2%. Nobody measured it, so nobody knew. It was rewritten and the worst case is now 7.1%, but the breach itself was never disclosed.

It is now defect 24. The instrument is allowed to excuse those releases — their history cannot be edited — but only while defect 24 is a numbered row in the register below. Remove the disclosure and the test goes red. An exception that outlives its own disclosure is a silenced test, and a silenced test is worse than no test.

The two instruments answer two questions and neither substitutes for the other. Is the reconstruction trustworthy? — thirty-three identical reads. Is the document improving? — thirty-three transitions, forward and backward. Both run before every release, and a failure in either stops the release.
rcore.version:
A version is a conversation, not an append

The ledger was counting its own edits and calling them versions. Those are two different numbers and only one of them is about the reader

Every block edit appends to the ledger, and the ledger numbers each append so that replay can find it. That number is a revision. It is a fact about the mechanism, it moves whenever anything is written, and it is necessary — without it there is nothing to replay to.

It is not what a reader means by a version. A reader means: the document I was handed, and answered. Those two numbers had been the same number, so the headline moved several times between one reading and the next, and appeared to describe progress that no reader had seen.

🔒 The rule · class: Immutable

A version increments once, when a delivered document has been read and answered. Everything written between two readings is one version, whether it took one revision or eleven. The revision count keeps running underneath and stays visible — it is the audit trail — but it no longer sets the headline.

RevisionVersion
Countsevery append to the ledgerevery delivered document that was answered
Moved bythe author, at willa reader, by responding
Answerswhat can I replay to?which document are we discussing?
Can it move without a reader?Yes, constantly.No. That is the entire point.
Nothing in the ledger is renumbered to make this true. Renumbering would change every state hash and break the replay this document is built on — and rewriting the record to flatter a count is the one thing forbidden here. The revisions stay exactly as written; the version is a second, slower counter laid over them.
⚠ What this cost, stated plainly

Three documents were written and numbered between one reading and the next. Under the corrected rule that is one version, and the numbering said three. A count that runs ahead of its readers is measuring effort rather than agreement, and this document is supposed to be about agreement.
rcore.plain:
Plain enough to be checked

A framework that asks the world to check its arithmetic, in sentences the world cannot get through, has picked the easy half of accountability

The instruction was given plainly: write so that a high-school reader can follow it. It went into the brief and nothing ever checked it. Every other promise in this document has an instrument — replay is proven thirty-three times, transitions are measured forward and backward, duplication is counted by shingle overlap, every section is counted to 333 words. The sentences themselves were never measured once.

⚠ The score, published because we fail it
Flesch-Kincaid grade, per section     bar 12 · target 10

mean grade                    13.5
over the bar                  16 of 20 sections
densest        §16 THE LEGAL PATHWAY    16.3   graduate reading
plainest       §19 WHAT WE ASK          8.9   on target

Grade 16 is a reader with a degree, most of the way through it. That is not “plainly enough” by any measure, and no amount of good intention in the drafting changes what the sentences actually do to a person trying to read them.

What §19 already proves

One section is on target, and it is the one that asks for something. §19 runs at grade 8.9 with an average sentence of seventeen words, while the document’s mean sentence is twenty-five. It is not shorter, and it is not simpler in what it claims. It is written in the voice a person uses when they actually want to be understood, because it is the only section with something to lose if it is not.

So the target is not theoretical and it does not require giving anything up. It requires writing the other eighteen the way the nineteenth was already written — short sentences carrying long thoughts, which is harder than the reverse and is the whole craft.

The rule, from here

No section over grade 12. Target grade 10. Measured by scripts/readability-vision2525.mjs on the rendered reading, published whether it flatters or not. It reports rather than blocks, deliberately: a gate that failed the build today would hide the number it exists to publish, and the number is the point until the rewriting is done.

Logged as defect 25 — not a wrong number this time, but a promise made and never instrumented, which is the quieter and more common failure.
paper.s6:
§6 · THE SETTLEMENT ↑ contents

§6   The Settlement

Extends §1

Every worker knows two days: the day the work is done and the day the work is paid. Between them lies a distance that has broken more households than idleness did. The shift is finished; the transfer clears next month, in a currency that moved while you slept. This is the oldest anxiety in labor — not whether the hour was real, but what it becomes by the time it reaches your hand. Any honest scheme of recognition must cross that distance, and the crossing is where such schemes die.

The design crosses it in two moments, deliberately kept apart. In the first moment an hour becomes recognition with no currency anywhere inside it: hours multiplied by a coefficient that is nothing but a division — the annual ceiling spread across a working year of two thousand and eighty hours, four point eight zero seven, identical on every continent because division holds no passport. In the second moment money appears: the place you earned and its statutory rate are written onto the entry once, and after that stamp nothing rewrites them — not a move, a law, or a rate. Your past keeps the price it carried while you lived it.

Say plainly what this does not equalize. The same two thousand and eighty hours settle near seven hundred seven dollars in Nigeria and fifteen thousand and eighty in Texas — multiply thirty-four cents by the year, then seven dollars and twenty-five cents, and you hold both figures without trusting us. Across the full register of one hundred and three jurisdictions the true spread is forty-seven point nine to one, worse than the figure long quoted from one convenient comparison — kept, because the uglier number is the stronger case for a currency-free mint. What the unit equalizes is duration: everyone reaches the ceiling on the same hours, while the local wage still decides what those hours buy at home. The stamping service is specified, not built; today there is only a table of rates and verification dates. Settlement arrives in stages: twenty-nine jurisdictions ready now, thirty-seven waiting only on data entry, thirty-five waiting on a published selection rule, thirteen with no statutory rate at all — payable through an agreed floor, so no one on earth settles at zero. A ladder, honestly labeled, is still a gap between promise and payout for everyone on its lower rungs today.

Every rate, floor, and band is a hand on a lever, and the guard is arithmetic, not trust. Criteria publish before the period they govern; changes bind only forward; appeals are heard outside the treasury that pays; the count of people in each band publishes every period. If the share of contributors reaching the ceiling drops below eight in ten, the tables publish with commentary; below six in ten, formal review; below four in ten, the authority freezes on its own. No one has to be brave. The number does the accusing.

You can audit this tonight without permission. Find the statutory minimum where you live. Multiply it by a full-time year and you have your floor income; divide the ceiling by those same hours and the coefficient falls out unchanged. Any figure that will not come out of your calculator twice is evidence — and it is yours to publish.

Needs

A unit minted in dollars imports the inequality it was built to remove, on the first day, invisibly. If the record of an hour is created already denominated in a currency, then the moment of creation has already ranked the world, and everything downstream inherits that ranking no matter how carefully it is governed. This is the failure that kills fairness mechanisms before they start: not a policy anyone chose. A default nobody examined.

Outcomes

An hour becomes a record without touching any currency at all. Jurisdiction and rate appear only at settlement, are stamped once, and are frozen for life, so a person who moves does not have their past re-priced by their present address. The record is made once and read forever. The money is a local translation of it, applied at the edge rather than baked into the core.

Solution

The register covers one hundred and three jurisdictions. Each entry carries a statutory rate and the date it was verified. At settlement — a service specified here and not yet built; today only the rate table exists as data — the earner’s jurisdiction and rate are written onto the ledger entry and never recalculated, which means a rate change next year cannot reach backwards into work already done. Mint currency-free, settle local, freeze on stamp.

Evidence

Building the register turned up something we had been publishing incorrectly for twenty-nine releases. We had been quoting a twenty-one-fold spread between the highest and lowest rates, which was the Texas-to-Nigeria comparison we happened to have started with. Across the full table it is forty-seven point nine. Priced by local wage the ceiling would take six hundred and fourteen hours in Washington State and twenty-nine thousand four hundred and nine in Nigeria; currency-free, 2,080 everywhere. A working life between them. We corrected the figure rather than the framing, because the larger number is the better argument for why the mint is currency-free in the first place. Thirteen jurisdictions still have no statutory rate at all and therefore no settlement path, which is a hole in the middle of the register and is listed in the open decisions as exactly that.

The separation

The stamp is the part that closes the arbitrage. Before, 웃 settled at whatever rate applied where the holder stood, so an hour earned in Lagos could be redeemed in Seattle at 47.9 times its origin. Now the earner’s jurisdiction and rate are written onto the append-only entry at mint and never re-resolved. There is no longer a trade to detect, because there is no longer a trade.

⚠ Found and closed inside the same release

The release-34 fix set the mint coefficient to 7.25 — a US dollar figure used as a token rate. It put a full-time year at 15,080 웃, overshooting the ceiling by 50.8%, and it silently contradicted the locked identity that one full-time year lands exactly on 9,999. The coefficient is now derived — 9,999 ÷ 2,080 = 4.807 — so the identity cannot drift, and a test asserts it rather than a comment claiming it. Logged as defect 15, opened and closed at release 35. Yesterday’s fix contained today’s defect; that is what the loop is for.
unit.guard:
Who sets the multiple

Introducing multiples introduces a control point, and it must be named before it is used rather than after it is abused.

⚠ Structural risk

Whoever sets the multiples controls the money. Every protection elsewhere in this framework can be routed around by an authority that simply reclassifies someone into a lower band.

Four guards, all classed Stable rather than Adaptive, because a number that can be changed quietly is not a number — it is a discretion:

  1. Bands are published in advance of the period they apply to, with the criteria for each band stated in plain language a contributor can check themselves against.
  2. Changes apply prospectively only. No retroactive reclassification of contribution already recorded.
  3. Assignment is appealable to a body that does not hold the budget the assignment draws on. An appeal decided by the payer is not an appeal.
  4. Distribution is published. How many people sit in each band, by region, every period. A treasury quietly rationing through band assignment appears immediately in that table.

Escalation

Guards without an escalation path are advisory. The reach rate is the tripwire and the ladder is published in advance:

reach_rate >= 0.80    normal operation
reach_rate <  0.80    band distribution published with commentary that period
reach_rate <  0.60    formal review of band criteria; outcome published
reach_rate <  0.40    band-setting authority suspended; bands frozen at prior period
                      until the governing council restores it on a published finding

The point of the ladder is that nobody has to allege anything. A falling reach rate triggers the next rung on its own, and the rung is visible to every contributor at the same moment it is visible to the authority that caused it.
livelihood.direct:
Livelihood — the ground beneath the work

The problem is old and simple: a person can do everything right and still be one bad month from losing their home — so their best work goes to managing fear instead of building. Livelihood keeps the ground steady: a place to live, a way to move, food, a phone — because a person who cannot lose their home does braver work.

Livelihood is a destination, not a token. A person directs value they have already earned toward the cost of living — home, mobility, food, communications, utilities. Nothing new is minted; nothing is held for them; no points become money.

Pay-Person-First

The money belongs to the person first. Earned 웃 is their compensation — recognized, classified and withheld — and then they choose where it goes. Sending it to a landlord or a lender changes the destination, never who earned it or what the law calls it.

Classify before delivery

Every payment is classified for tax, payroll and law before it moves. The framework only instructs; a licensed rail moves the money; Replay proves each step. Vision 2525 never holds or transmits funds.

Two ways carry it. The steady way is in kind: where the framework or a project owns the home or the vehicle and lets a contributor use it as a working condition, that can be lawful in kind rather than a taxed allowance. The flexible way is taxed cash, sent after withholding to the providers a person picks. Necessities first; the rest is theirs. Each country’s version is signed off by counsel before any real money moves.
bonus.bridge:
The bridge — recognition becomes a reward, never a currency

Being early, being generous, wielding a tool well — these should count for something. The moment recognition becomes money you can hold or trade, it turns into a security and a tax mess. The bridge lets it count without ever becoming currency.

The bridge

Recognition never turns into cash. It only makes a person eligible. When they qualify, a separate, separately-funded Bonus may be awarded under Human Authority and classified under law before it pays. Points never buy a house; qualified contribution can make a person eligible for a housing bonus, and the bonus is then paid.

Recognition gates the bonus, never the bed. A home under Livelihood comes from a person’s role — the working condition — not from any tally of points.

Home Continuity Bonus

A qualified person may become eligible for a housing award toward a down payment or closing — a bonus designed to vest when the home closes and pay soon after, wired by a licensed processor to the closing agent on the person’s instruction; the exact forfeiture and timing are reviewed by counsel under applicable law. A lender or underwriter stays the independent authority and may say no; the bridge never overrides them. In a lease-to-own home the same builds as a purchase-price credit — a real stake in the property, never a balance to cash out.

Being early is rewarded the way loyalty is; every dollar arrives as a lawful, classified payment to the person who earned it.
paper.s7:
§7 · THE OFF SWITCH ↑ contents

§7   The Off Switch

Extends §1

Anyone who has written a will knows the strange calm that follows. Nothing about death changed; only the ending stopped being something that would happen to the people you love and became something you had handled for them. You end a conversation before it curdles, a job before it hollows you, and the endings you chose you can stand behind, while the endings that chose you still ache. Institutions feel none of this and look away from their own mortality — which is why every one you watched die did so late, ugly, and in the hands of whoever stood nearest the money.

So the ending is arithmetic before it is drama. One enrolled person in a thousand can open the question — small enough that dissent cannot be smothered, large enough that one bad week cannot start a funeral. Forty of every hundred must show up, because absence is not consent to anything. Sixty of every hundred ballots must say stop, because ending a shared thing weighs more than steering it. The whole count runs again half a year later, because fury is seasonal and endings should not be. Test each figure yourself: every threshold sits near the smallest value that defeats its own abuse.

The money submits to the same discipline. Whoever funded the reserve is repaid at the figure frozen on the day they gave, and the people already owed are made whole before any funder sees anything, because a promise that dissolves the moment keeping it turns expensive was only ever a mood. The funders cast the same single ballot as anyone who never gave a cent — the one place where generosity purchases no leverage, kept costly on purpose. Whatever goes unclaimed waits inside a locked trust only a restart can open, and the length of the sleep — one, two, or three years — falls out of a hash any stranger can recompute, so no faction can time the resurrection.

Now the two deaths of the mechanism itself. Seized: the keys to this most valuable lever are held apart — a mandate from everyone, a council supermajority, a founder counter-signature able only to slow a stop and never to start one, and a ceremony whose secret the software cannot read. Rusted: a switch guarded too well stops being a switch, so the veto dies of silence after ninety days, dies with its holder, and expires by the calendar over every objection. Be exact about the present tense. The thresholds remain proposals, so today the switch is drawn in full and wired to nothing; how a person with no papers casts one ballot and never two is still left unsolved; the payout formula, as written, rewards abandoning a sinking system — a spiral the record names rather than paints over.

None of this asks for your trust, which is the design. This week, put one question to every institution holding your money or your years: where is the written procedure for its ending? Notice how rarely an answer exists, and who profits from the blank. Then take whatever you run — a team, a fund, a household — and draft its exit terms now, while you still love it, because terms written in affection are the only ones that stay fair after affection runs out.

Needs

A system that cannot be ended must be trusted forever, and nothing should be trusted forever — not this framework, not its authors, not the page you are reading.

This is the point at which most ambitious frameworks quietly assume their own permanence, usually by never mentioning termination. But an institution with no shutdown procedure has not avoided the question of its ending; it has merely guaranteed that when the ending comes it will be disorderly, and that whoever is holding the assets at that moment will decide what happens to them. You would not sign a contract with no exit clause. This section is that clause, written first.

Outcomes

You can switch this off. Not a metaphor: any enrolled person may petition, the vote is one person one vote, and nothing anyone has contributed — including money — buys a heavier ballot. Humanity ends this deliberately, with the money already accounted for.

Not a collapse and not a crisis: a vote, a formula published before anyone needed it, and a wind-down that runs the same whether the people running it are still enthusiastic or not. A framework that publishes its own termination in advance is easier to trust precisely because it has less to lose by being honest.

Solution

The vote is one person, one vote, unweighted, requiring two-thirds consensus and counter-signature by the Innovation Leader under a master credential held in one place. On shutdown every Seed Token is swapped back at its own vintage price — the figure frozen when it was issued — so nobody receives more than they contributed and nobody receives less. Residue enters a Trust that can only be reopened if the system is restarted.

Dormancy runs one to three years. Restart requires submitted improvements and unanimity on the date, so coming back is deliberately harder than stopping. Ending this is not a death; it is a forced learning cycle with a real cost attached.

Evidence

What this is, stated plainly: an institution that publishes its own death certificate in advance. No state writes the procedure for its own dissolution while it is healthy, and no company publishes the vote that ends it. We are writing it at the beginning, while we are the people it would be used against, which is the only moment the terms can be honest.

The guarantee survives the vote. If you are mid-payout, you continue to be paid through a shutdown — an obligation that evaporates when the institution becomes inconvenient was never an obligation.

Three things here are unresolved and published as such: the five shutdown thresholds are unratified, and whether reserves should be fully pre-funded or duration-matched is an open fork with real consequences either way. The third is identity: how a natural person with no documents is counted once, and only once, in the one-person, one-vote ballot. We could have written plausible numbers into the first two. We wrote neither, on the principle that a specific number nobody has agreed to is worse than an admitted gap — the gap invites a decision, and you are among the people it invites.
off.switch:
The right to switch it off

The asymmetry this closes

Five shields exist to stop anyone else ending this system. Until release 37 there was no way for the people inside it to end it. That is the exact shape of every institution that outlived its usefulness and could not be stopped — and we built it by accident while congratulating ourselves on the shields.

Any natural person may petition to switch the system off. The vote is sovereignty class, which under the wall (r19) means unweighted, one person one vote. It is not prioritisation, so the quadratic weighting and the 15% cap do not apply, and neither does anything anyone contributed.

⚠ Seed Token holders get no extra vote on this

The people who funded the reserve are the people the reserve pays out to when it closes — and they vote on the shutdown with exactly the same single vote as someone who has never given a cent. This is the first place in thirty-seven releases where “money receives, it does not decide” costs somebody something real. If that rule is ever going to be quietly softened, it will be softened here.

● What this actually is

Every mechanism above is machinery. The claim underneath it is not.

This is an institution that publishes its own death certificate in advance.

No state writes the procedure for its own dissolution while it is healthy. No company publishes the vote that ends it. The reason is not oversight — it is that an institution which can be ended is an institution that must keep earning its existence, and most would rather not sign up for that. So the procedure gets written, if ever, by whoever is left when the thing is already failing, which is the worst possible moment and the worst possible authors.

We are writing it now, at the beginning, while nobody wants to use it and while we are the people it would be used against. That is the only moment the terms can be honest. A framework that argues for its own permanence has already told you what it values more than the people it serves.

And the commitment is asymmetric on purpose. The five shields make this hard for outsiders to end. This section makes it possible for its own people to end. Anyone who reads those two together and finds them contradictory has understood them exactly: the framework is defended against everyone except the humans inside it, who need no defence against because they are who it is for.

Thresholds — proposed, not ratified

GateProposedWhy this shape
Petition to open a vote0.1% of enrolled personsLow enough that dissent cannot be gatekept; high enough that it is not one person’s bad week.
Quorum40% of enrolledA minority cannot end it through everyone else’s absence.
Carry60% of votes castEnding is a sovereign act. A bare majority is not enough; unanimity is a veto for the complacent.
Confirmationrepeat vote, 180 days laterThe same result twice, half a year apart. One angry season cannot do it.
Effect90 days after confirmationTime to close sessions, settle 웃 in flight, and publish the final state.
These five numbers are a proposal awaiting ratification, in the same state as the three decisions at release 31. Until the councils set them, the switch is a specified mechanism rather than a live one, and the defect register says so.

Switch-off is Immutable class as a right and Adaptive class as a number: the ability to end the system can never be removed, amended away, or made conditional on anyone’s permission. The thresholds above can be changed by the ordinary process. The right cannot.
off.keys:
Who can turn the key

⚠ A deliberate exception to our own principle, named rather than harmonised

Release 37 made switch-off sovereignty class: unweighted, one person one vote. This release gives one named person a counter-signature over that vote — an exception, made on purpose, written down as one. Three things make it survivable: it is a brake and never a throttle, it expires, and it lapses on silence.

Three gates

GateWhoClassBar
1Mandate — every enrolled natural personSovereignty · unweighted 1p1v40% quorum, 60% carry, confirmed 180 days later (r37)
2Counter-signature — the tri-council, the Innovation Leader among themConsensusTwo-thirds of council, Leader’s assent inside that two-thirds
3Execution — the master admin accountCeremony, not a decisionTwo keys: identity, then a secret the application cannot read
Gate 3 carries out a choice already made by everyone else.
A brake, never a throttle

The counter-signature can only stop or slow a shutdown — never start one. No combination of the Leader and council can end this system without a carried mandate from ordinary people. The single asymmetry that makes a one-person veto tolerable.

The First Innovation Term, and its zero

The counter-signature belongs to the First Innovation Term — the founding 7 + 3 standing, seven years leading with full authority, three mentoring with none:

t0 = the moment cumulative Seed Token proceeds reach $1,000,000 not incorporation. not the first commit. a checkable on-ledger event. t0 + 7 years leading, counter-signature live t0 + 10 years standing ends; counter-signature LAPSES AUTOMATICALLY gate 2 becomes tri-council two-thirds, alone, forever after

One million tokens is one million people. The term ends on a computable day; no vote, amendment or emergency extends it.

When the counter-signature lapses early

ConditionEffectWhy
No response within 90 days of a carried mandateLapses for that petition; gate 2 proceeds on council two-thirds aloneAn off switch disabled by not answering the phone is not an off switch.
Death, or incapacity certified by the councilLapses immediately and permanentlyNo single point of failure that biology can trigger.
Recall under the r33 processLapses with the standingEvery office here has a removal path.
End of the First Innovation TermLapses automatically at t0 + 10 yearsOne decade of benefit of the doubt. Not one day more.

The two-key ceremony — protocol only

✓ The secret is not in this document, this repository, or any log

The master PIN is held by the Leader and appears nowhere in the system it unlocks. Verified: zero tracked files contain it, a condition of every future release.

The application never sees the stored secret; the comparison is against a salted Argon2id hash; the ceremony writes an append-only audit row — who, when, against which mandate, never what they typed. A failed ceremony is as permanently recorded as a successful one.

⚠ Two things a reader should not take on trust

An eight-digit numeric PIN is 100,000,000 combinations — minutes of brute force without a lockout, which is why the lockout is part of the specification. And a PIN typed into a live session is not really a second factor: whoever holds the session can type it. The second factor must be bound to hardware. Logged as defects 18 and 19.
off.reserve:
What happens to the reserve

At switch-off the reserve does not become a pot to be divided. It splits three ways, in strict order, and the first claim is not a shareholder’s.

✓ The guarantee outlives the vote

Someone two years into an elected five-year payout does not lose the remaining three because a vote went a certain way. Obligations already earned are discharged in full before a single Seed Token is repaid. “Paid out over the elected term, guaranteed” means nothing if a majority can cancel it, and the shutdown is precisely where that promise would be cheapest to break. This uses the existing headroom = reserve − committed term from release 30 rather than a new one.

The Continuity Index

Each holder receives a share of the holder pool proportional to the increase across the four metrics between the year they bought and the year the system stops. Four metrics, equally weighted: Revenue · Gross Profit · Operating Income · R&D Spend.

for each metric m:   Δm(y) = m(y_off) − m(y_bought)
                    share_m(y) = Δm(y) / Δm(y_first)

Index(y) = Σ w_m · share_m(y)      w = 0.25 each
claim(h) = tokens(h) × Index(year_bought(h))
payout(h) = claim(h) / Σclaims × holder_pool
Why differences and not ratios

The obvious reading is a growth ratio, m(y_off) / m(y_bought). It breaks immediately: operating income is negative in the early years of anything worth building, and the ratio at year zero comes out at −144.0 — a number with no meaning that would silently invert an early founder’s claim. Differences are well defined through zero, run cleanly from 1.0000 for the founding year to 0.0000 for someone who bought on the day it stopped, and are monotone in between.

Worked example — illustrative figures, real arithmetic

HolderBoughtTokensIndexPayout
Adaezeyear 11000.9958$33,364,877
Sokhayear 4100.9108$3,051,776
Mireilleyear 81,0000.5902$197,745,879
Tomasyear 111000.1742$5,837,468
Twelve operating years; the four metrics grow from $2.0M / $1.2M / −$0.5M / $1.5M to $480M / $312M / $72M / $96M. Mireille holds ten times Adaeze’s tokens and takes the largest share; Adaeze earns $333,649 per token against Tomas’s $58,375 for arriving ten years later. That ratio is the mechanism working exactly as specified.
⚠ Defect 16, published in the release that creates it

That same ratio is dangerous. A holder who buys in the final year receives almost nothing; a holder who buys in the shutdown year receives exactly zero and loses their entire contribution. So if shutdown ever begins to look likely, the rational act is to stop funding — which drains the reserve, which makes shutdown likelier. The rule is self-fulfilling at precisely the moment the system most needs money.

Proposed guard, awaiting ratification: return of principal first, pro rata if the pool cannot cover it, then the index-weighted split of whatever remains. Late holders stop being wiped out; early holders keep the whole of the upside they actually generated. This preserves the operator’s rule for the surplus and only floors the downside — but it is a change to a stated instruction, so it is proposed here rather than assumed.
off.trust:
The Continuity Trust, and the years of silence

What the holders do not claim does not revert to anyone. It goes into a Continuity Trust — asset-locked, under the same terms as Shield II, with a single permitted use: funding a restart. No trustee may distribute it, borrow against it, or spend it on anything else, and no one may wind it up.

There is a quiet justice in how it is funded. The Trust is built from the shares of the people who did not come back to claim them — which is, near enough, the people a restart would be for.

Dormancy is drawn, not chosen

At switch-off a dormancy of one, two or three years is selected by seeded draw from the final state hash. Nothing may restart before it expires.

D = ( sha256( "vision2525:shutdown:" + final_state_hash ) mod 3 ) + 1

   2464687d0e3dee896162ef1209e71244...  ->  D = 2 years
   earliest restart = D + 1  =  3 years after switch-off
Why a coin and not a committee

A chosen dormancy would be negotiated, and a known restart date would be organised around: capital parked against it, coalitions assembled for it, the restart timed to a political season rather than a readiness. A drawn one cannot be. The draw is deterministic and publishable, so anyone can verify it was not fixed — the same seeded-hash discipline this document uses for replay, applied to the one number nobody should be able to influence.

The extra year on top of the draw is not delay for its own sake. It is the preparation window: the period in which the improvement mandate below is actually compiled, compressed, ranked and signed. Dormancy is when the system is off. The year after it is when the work of deserving to come back gets done.
off.restart:
Coming back

A restart is not a reversal. Reversing a shutdown would make the vote theatre — a pause anyone could wait out. Three conditions, all of which must hold:

#ConditionWhat it prevents
1The dormancy has expired and the preparation year has run — earliest D+1.Waiting out a decision instead of accepting it.
2A single agreed effective date. The restart petition carries one date; the vote is on that exact date. No date, no vote.A restart that passes with no one agreeing when it happens.
3The Improvement Mandate. Every petitioner submits at least one concrete change to make the system better. Nothing restarts without them.Restarting the system that was rejected, unchanged, and expecting a different result.

The Improvement Mandate

Submitted changes are not a wish list stapled to a petition. They enter the loop this framework already runs, unmodified:

collect (Cube 22, 33 languages)  ->  compress (Cube 6, deterministic)
  ->  rank (Cube 7, capped 15%)  ->  certify (Cube 12)  ->  sign (Cube 25, a person)
  ->  the restarted corpus
✓ The condition is machine-checkable

The restarted release must differ from the switched-off release in at least one ratified block, and the difference must be publishable. That is not a promise anyone has to trust — it is a compare(v_off, v_restart) call, which is the control built in release 36. If it returns zero added and zero revised, the restart is void. The tool that shows a reader what changed turns out to be the enforcement mechanism for whether a change happened at all.

Only on a valid restart does the Continuity Trust open, and only into the reserve — never into anyone’s hands. Holders who were paid out at shutdown are not repaid or reinstated; their tenure ended when the system did. A restarted system raises its Seed again, from whoever believes in the improved version, which is the only honest way to find out whether the improvements are real.

What the switch actually is

Read together, these four sections are not an exit. They are a forced learning cycle with a real cost attached. Ending the system is permitted, survivable, and expensive; coming back is permitted, delayed, and conditional on having learned something. A framework that intends to run for five hundred years will be wrong at some point along the way, probably more than once. This is the mechanism by which being wrong is recoverable instead of terminal — and the reason it can be built at all is that nothing here is stored. It is replayed. A system that can reconstruct any state it has ever held can afford to stop, because stopping does not erase it.
paper.s8:
§8 · WHAT WE CANNOT SEE ↑ contents

§8   What We Cannot See

Extends §5

There is an experiment you may have done as a child. Draw a small dot on a page, hold it at arm’s length, cover one eye, and move the page slowly — at a certain distance the dot vanishes.
